metadata.title: Normalisers of parabolic subgroups of Artin–Tits groups and Tits cone intersections
metadata.description: Research article: Normalisers of parabolic subgroups of Artin–Tits groups and Tits cone intersections
summary: Let (W, S) be a Coxeter system and let J ⊆S. Motivated by 3-fold flops, Iyama and Wemyss study the hyperplane arrangement in the Tits cone intersection of J, which is a J- relative generalisation of the classical Coxeter arrangement. For Γ of spherical type, the authors show that the complexified complement of this J-relative hyperplane arrangement is a K(π, 1) space for the normaliser (quotient) of the standard parabolic subgroup attached to J in the Artin–Tits group.

For general Γ the authors show that the Brink–Howlett groupoid, which describes normalisers of parabolic subgroups of the Coxeter groups, has its universal cover described by the wall-and-chamber structure of the Tits cone intersection. The authors use this to show that wall crossing sequences satisfy an “atomic Matsumoto relation”, generalising a theorem of Ko and answering questions raised by Iyama and Wemyss.

cex-relative-not-reflection-artin-tits-n.title: A relative arrangement need not be a reflection arrangement

statement.heading: Counterexample
statement.source_excerpt:
**Proof technique:** direct.

**Given:** The $D_4$ system with central vertex $2$ and $J=\{2\}$, with its relative arrangement as in [F1] and [F2].

**Goal:** Prove that this arrangement is irreducible and cannot be a finite real reflection arrangement.

1.1 Suppose the arrangement has a product decomposition $E=E_1\oplus E_2$ with both summands nonzero. The dual decomposes as $E^*=E_1^*\oplus E_2^*$, where each summand is extended by zero on the other space. By the product condition, a nonzero defining form for each hyperplane belongs to one of these two dual summands: forms with the same kernel are nonzero scalar multiples. In particular $x$, $y$ and $z$ each lie in one summand. Since $x+y$ also lies in one summand, uniqueness of the two components in the direct sum forces $x$ and $y$ to lie in the same summand. The same argument with $x+z$ puts $z$ there too. But $x,y,z$ form a basis of $E^*$, so the other dual summand is zero, contrary to both $E_1$ and $E_2$ being nonzero. Thus the arrangement is irreducible. [F1, F3, given]

2.1 By [F1] the arrangement has seven hyperplanes in dimension three. If it were a finite real reflection arrangement, its irreducibility from 1.1 would make [F4] applicable, requiring its number of hyperplanes to be $6$, $9$ or $15$. Since $7$ is none of these, it is not a finite real reflection arrangement. This example therefore refutes the asserted universal property. [F1, F4, step 1.1] ∎

cor-coxeter-normaliser-splitting-artin-t.title: Coxeter normaliser semidirect product

statement.heading: Statement
statement.source_excerpt:
Let $(W,S)$ be an arbitrary-rank Coxeter system with $S=\{s_i:i\in\Gamma_0\}$ in its standard real root representation, and let $J\subseteq\Gamma_0$ be arbitrary. Write $W_J=\langle s_j:j\in J\rangle$, $M=\operatorname{Norm}_W(W_J)$ and $N(W,J)=M/W_J$. Let $N_J=\mathcal{BH}_J$ be the vertex group at $J$, equivalently the subgroup permuting the simple-root set $\{\alpha_j:j\in J\}$.

The vertex group $N_J$ maps isomorphically onto $N(W,J)$ under the normaliser quotient, and $\mathrm{Norm}_W(W_J)\cong W_J\rtimes N_J$.

cor-deligne-normal-cover-artin-tits-norm.title: Normal Deligne–ribbon cover and its deck group

statement.heading: Statement
statement.source_excerpt:
Let $(W,S)$ be a finite-rank spherical Coxeter system, meaning that $W$ is finite, and fix $J\subseteq S$. Write $W_J$ for the subgroup generated by $J$ and $N=N(W,J)=\operatorname{Norm}_W(W_J)/W_J$. Let $\mathcal D$ be the relative arrangement groupoid and $\mathcal R$ the reduced ribbon groupoid. With the functors $\mathcal G:\mathcal D\to\mathcal R$ and $\mathcal Q:\mathcal D\to\mathcal D/N$ of [def-deligne-ribbon-mapping-artin-tits-normalisers](item-def-deligne-ribbon-mapping-artin-tits-normalisers), there is an isomorphism of groupoids $\mathcal G':\mathcal D/N\to\mathcal R$ satisfying $\mathcal G=\mathcal G'\circ\mathcal Q$.

The coverings $\mathcal Q$ and $\mathcal G$ are isomorphic via the identity on $\mathcal D$ and $\mathcal G'$ on their targets. In particular, $\mathcal G$ is a normal covering and its deck transformation group is isomorphic to $N$ via the action of $N$ on $\mathcal D$. A covering is a functor with a unique lift from each specified source object for every arrow starting at its image; a deck transformation is an automorphism of the source groupoid over the functor. Normality means that deck transformations act transitively on a fibre.

cor-geodesic-matsumoto-artin-tits-normal.title: Geodesics differ by codimension-two relations

statement.heading: Statement
statement.source_excerpt:
Let $(W,S)$ be a finite-rank Coxeter system with diagram vertex set $\Gamma_0$, and fix $J\subseteq\Gamma_0$. Write $W_L$ for the subgroup generated by the simple reflections indexed by $L$. Let $\Theta$ be the dual of the real geometric representation, let $\Theta_J$ be the subspace annihilating the simple roots indexed by $J$, and let $\mathrm{Cone}(J)^\circ$ be the interior in $\Theta_J$ of the intersection of $\Theta_J$ with the Tits cone. The relative arrangement $\mathcal H^J$ consists of the distinct restrictions to $\Theta_J$ of root hyperplanes not containing $\Theta_J$.

A chamber is a connected component of the complement of these hyperplanes in $\mathrm{Cone}(J)^\circ$; chambers are adjacent when they share a wall, a codimension-one intersection of a chamber closure with an arrangement hyperplane. A chamber path is a finite nonempty sequence of adjacent chambers, and it is geodesic when its number of crossings is minimal among paths with the same endpoints. The chamber labels $(x,I)$ belong to $\mathrm{Cham}(J)$: thus $W_Jx=xW_I$ and $x$ has minimum Coxeter length in $xW_I$.

A codimension-two relation replaces one of the two geodesic paths supplied by [def-codimension-two-artin-tits-normalisers](item-def-codimension-two-artin-tits-normalisers) by the other, with the same endpoints, inside a longer path. Any two geodesic paths $p,p':(x,I)\to(y,K)$ in $(\mathrm{Cone}(J)^\circ,\mathcal H^J)$ are related by a finite sequence of codimension-two relations.

cor-normaliser-kpi-artin-tits-normaliser.title: Spherical normaliser quotient classifying spaces

statement.heading: Statement
statement.source_excerpt:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $(W,S)$ be a finite-rank spherical Coxeter system, meaning that $W$ is finite, and let $J\subseteq S$. Let $A$ be the associated Artin–Tits group and $P$ the kernel of its standard projection to $W$. For $G=W,A$, let $G_J$ be the standard parabolic subgroup generated by the generators indexed by $J$, and put $N(G,J)=\operatorname{Norm}_G(G_J)/G_J$, where the normaliser consists of the elements conjugating $G_J$ to itself. Let $N(P,J)$ be the image of $P\cap\operatorname{Norm}_A(A_J)$ in $N(A,J)$.

Let $X=\mathcal X_J^{\mathbb C}$ be the relative complexified hyperplane complement. The induced action of $N(W,J)$ gives a quotient $X/N(W,J)$. Then $X$ is a $K(N(P,J),1)$ and $X/N(W,J)$ is a $K(N(A,J),1)$. Here $K(G,1)$ means a path-connected space whose fundamental group is isomorphic to $G$ and whose homotopy groups in all degrees at least two vanish.

def-arrangement-groupoids-artin-tits-nor.title: Positive arrangement category and its groupoid completion

statement.heading: Definition
statement.source_excerpt:
Fix a finite-rank Coxeter system and a subset $J$ of its vertices. Let $(\mathrm{Cone}(J)^\circ,\mathcal H^J)$ be its relative arrangement, and let $\mathrm{Cham}(J)$ be its set of chambers, the connected components of the arrangement complement. Two distinct chambers are adjacent when they share a wall, a codimension-one intersection of a chamber closure with an arrangement hyperplane.

Form the directed graph $Q_J$ with vertex set $\mathrm{Cham}(J)$ and exactly one arrow $C\to C'$ for each ordered pair of adjacent chambers. Thus each adjacent pair gives two oppositely directed arrows. A path is a finite sequence of composable arrows; the empty path at $C$ has source and target $C$. Its length is the number of arrows. A path is **geodesic** if its length is minimal among paths with the same source and target.

Let $R_J$ consist of all pairs of geodesic paths with the same source and target. The **positive arrangement category** $\mathcal D^+(J)$ is the category presented by $Q_J$ and $R_J$: its objects are the chambers and its morphisms are paths modulo the smallest endpoint-preserving equivalence relation containing $R_J$ and stable under concatenation on either side. Composition is induced by concatenation, read from left to right; empty paths give identities.

The **arrangement groupoid** $\mathcal D(J)$ is the groupoid completion of $\mathcal D^+(J)$, obtained by formally adjoining inverses to its morphisms. Its canonical functor from $\mathcal D^+(J)$ is universal for functors into groupoids. In spherical type, meaning that the Coxeter group is finite, the article calls $\mathcal D(J)$ the **Deligne groupoid**.

statement.heading: Definition
statement.source_excerpt:
Fix a finite-rank Coxeter system and a subset $J$ of its vertices. Let $(\mathrm{Cone}(J)^\circ,\mathcal H^J)$ be its relative arrangement, and let $\mathrm{Cham}(J)$ be its set of chambers, the connected components of the arrangement complement. Two distinct chambers are adjacent when they share a wall, a codimension-one intersection of a chamber closure with an arrangement hyperplane.

Form the directed graph $Q_J$ with vertex set $\mathrm{Cham}(J)$ and exactly one arrow $C\to C'$ for each ordered pair of adjacent chambers. Thus each adjacent pair gives two oppositely directed arrows. A path is a finite sequence of composable arrows; the empty path at $C$ has source and target $C$. Its length is the number of arrows. A path is **geodesic** if its length is minimal among paths with the same source and target.

Let $R_J$ consist of all pairs of geodesic paths with the same source and target. The **positive arrangement category** $\mathcal D^+(J)$ is the category presented by $Q_J$ and $R_J$: its objects are the chambers and its morphisms are paths modulo the smallest endpoint-preserving equivalence relation containing $R_J$ and stable under concatenation on either side. Composition is induced by concatenation, read from left to right; empty paths give identities.

The **arrangement groupoid** $\mathcal D(J)$ is the groupoid completion of $\mathcal D^+(J)$, obtained by formally adjoining inverses to its morphisms. Its canonical functor from $\mathcal D^+(J)$ is universal for functors into groupoids. In spherical type, meaning that the Coxeter group is finite, the article calls $\mathcal D(J)$ the **Deligne groupoid**.

def-arrangement-topology-interface-artin.title: Locally finite arrangements and relative face terminology

statement.heading: Definition
statement.source_excerpt:
Let $E$ be a finite-dimensional real vector space, let $n=\dim_{\mathbb R}E$, and choose a linear coordinate isomorphism $c:E\to\mathbb R^n$. On $\mathbb R^n$ use the Euclidean metric $d_2(u,v)=(\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}(u_i-v_i)^2)^{1/2}$. Give $E$ the metric $d_E(x,y)=d_2(c(x),c(y))$ and its metric topology: $O\subseteq E$ is open if for each $x\in O$ there is $r>0$ such that $\{y\in E:d_E(x,y)<r\}\subseteq O$. For $n=0$, $\mathbb R^0$ and $E$ are singletons, the sum is empty and the metric is zero; the topology is $\{\varnothing,E\}$. This specifies the transported Euclidean topology. A subset $T\subseteq E$ is convex if $(1-t)x+ty\in T$ whenever $x,y\in T$ and $0\leq t\leq1$. Give $T$ the subspace topology: its open sets are the intersections of $T$ with open subsets of $E$. A neighbourhood of $x\in T$ is a subset of $T$ containing an open subset of $T$ that contains $x$.

An arrangement $(T,\mathcal A)$ consists of such a convex $T$ and a set $\mathcal A$ of linear hyperplanes $H\subseteq E$, each meeting $T$. A linear hyperplane is a linear subspace of codimension one. The arrangement is locally finite in $T$ if every $x\in T$ has a neighbourhood meeting only finitely many distinct members of $\mathcal A$. For a convex $T'\subseteq T$, its restriction has hyperplane set $\{H\in\mathcal A:H\cap T'\ne\varnothing\}$.

A chamber is a connected component of $T\setminus\bigcup_{H\in\mathcal A}H$, with the subspace topology. For a chamber $C$, write $\overline C$ for its closure in $E$: the points whose every open neighbourhood in $E$ meets $C$. An affine subspace of $E$ is a translate $a+U$ of a linear subspace $U\subseteq E$. Its direction space is $U=(a+U)-a$, and its affine dimension is $\dim_{\mathbb R}U$. For a nonempty set $A\subseteq E$, its affine hull $\operatorname{aff}(A)$ is the intersection of all affine subspaces containing $A$; its affine dimension is the affine dimension of $\operatorname{aff}(A)$. A wall of $C$ is a nonempty set $\overline C\cap H$ of affine dimension $\dim_{\mathbb R}E-1$, where $H\in\mathcal A$. No affine dimension is assigned to an empty intersection here. The wall is the intersection, while $H$ is its defining arrangement hyperplane; these are different kinds of objects. Two distinct chambers are adjacent if they share a wall. A gallery is a finite sequence of chambers in which consecutive chambers are adjacent; its length is the number of consecutive pairs.

A basis of a vector space is a linearly independent spanning set. An open simplicial cone in a finite-dimensional real vector space $F$ is a set $\{\sum_{i=1}^k t_i v_i:t_i>0\}$ for a basis $v_1,\ldots,v_k$ of $F$; for $k=0$ the empty sum is $0$. For an arrangement with $T=E$, put $L=\bigcap_{H\in\mathcal A}H$, taking $L=E$ when $\mathcal A$ is empty. The quotient vector space $E/L$ consists of cosets $x+L$ with operations $(x+L)+(y+L)=(x+y)+L$ and $t(x+L)=tx+L$; its canonical projection is $q:E\to E/L$, $q(x)=x+L$. The arrangement is simplicial if every chamber is of the form $L+\{\sum_{i=1}^k t_i v_i:t_i>0\}$, where $q(v_1),\ldots,q(v_k)$ form a basis of $E/L$. Thus the common linear factor is retained in $E$ and removed for the simplicial test.

def-artin-pure-lifts-artin-tits-normalis.title: Artin–Tits group, pure subgroup and positive lifts

statement.heading: Definition
statement.source_excerpt:
Let $(W,S)$ be a Coxeter system with $S=\{s_i:i\in\Gamma_0\}$ finite, and let $\mathcal X^{\mathbb C}$ be its classical complexified hyperplane complement. Choose $Z\in\mathcal X^{\mathbb C}$ and write $\overline Z$ for its orbit in $\mathcal X^{\mathbb C}/W$. The Artin–Tits group is $A=\pi_1(\mathcal X^{\mathbb C}/W,\overline Z)$, the group of based loop-homotopy classes in the quotient. The pure Artin–Tits group is $P=\pi_1(\mathcal X^{\mathbb C},Z)$, identified with its image in $A$ under the covering map. Let $\pi:A\to W$ send a loop class to the unique $w$ for which its lift starting at $Z$ ends at $wZ$.

Fix an isomorphism over $W$ from the presented Artin group to $A$ supplied by the fundamental-group identification. The presented group has generators $a_s$ for $s\in S$ and, for distinct $s,t$ with finite $m(s,t)=\operatorname{ord}(st)$, the relation equating the two alternating words of length $m(s,t)$ beginning with $a_s$ and $a_t$ respectively. Write $\sigma_s\in A$ for the image of $a_s$, and $\sigma_i=\sigma_{s_i}$. For a reduced expression $w=s_1\cdots s_r$, meaning an expression of minimum length among words in $S$ representing $w$, define the positive lift $\sigma_w=\sigma_{s_1}\cdots\sigma_{s_r}$; the empty product is the identity. Thus $w\mapsto\sigma_w$ is a set-theoretic section of $\pi$.

def-associates-artin-tits-normalisers.title: Associates of a parabolic subset

statement.heading: Definition
statement.source_excerpt:
Let $\Gamma$ be a Coxeter diagram with vertex set $\Gamma_0$ and associated Coxeter group $W$, with simple generators $s_i$ indexed by $i\in\Gamma_0$ as in [def-coxeter-data-artin-tits-normalisers](item-def-coxeter-data-artin-tits-normalisers). For $K\subseteq\Gamma_0$, let $W_K=\langle s_k:k\in K\rangle$ be its standard parabolic subgroup, as in [def-parabolic-subgroups-artin-tits-normalisers](item-def-parabolic-subgroups-artin-tits-normalisers).

For $J\subseteq\Gamma_0$, an **associate** of $J$ is a subset $I\subseteq\Gamma_0$ for which $W_I$ and $W_J$ are conjugate in $W$: that is, there exists $w\in W$ such that $W_I=wW_Jw^{-1}=\{wuw^{-1}:u\in W_J\}$.

def-atomic-braid-artin-tits-normalisers.title: Atomic braid relations

statement.heading: Definition
statement.source_excerpt:
Let $(W,S)$ be a Coxeter system with diagram vertex set $\Gamma_0$, simple generators $s_i$ and Coxeter length $\ell$. Fix $J\subseteq\Gamma_0$. For $L\subseteq\Gamma_0$, let $W_L=\langle s_i:i\in L\rangle$ and let $\Phi_L=\{w\alpha_i:w\in W_L,\ i\in L\}$ be its parabolic root set in the geometric representation. A subset $I$ is an associate of $J$ when $W_I$ is conjugate to $W_J$ in $W$.

Let $I$ be an associate of $J$ and let distinct $a,b\in\Gamma_0\setminus I$ satisfy $|\Phi_{I\cup\{a,b\}}\setminus\Phi_I|<\infty$. In the Brink–Howlett groupoid $\mathcal{BH}(J)$, whose objects are associates of $J$ and whose composable morphism labels multiply from left to right, let $v_{a,b,I}:I\to K$ be the common left multiple supplied by the two-generator lemma. Here left divisibility means $u\leq w$ if $w=uz$ and $\ell(w)=\ell(u)+\ell(z)$.

A standard expression is a composable product of elementary wall-crossing morphisms $v_{c,L}$ whose Coxeter lengths sum to the length of the product. The two-generator lemma supplies exactly two such expressions for $v_{a,b,I}$, one starting with $v_{a,I}$ and the other with $v_{b,I}$. Write them as

$$v_{a,b,I}=v_{a_1,I_1}\cdots v_{a_m,I_m}=v_{b_1,L_1}\cdots v_{b_m,L_m},$$

where $a_1=a$, $b_1=b$, and $I_1=L_1=I$. The equality

$$v_{a_1,I_1}\cdots v_{a_m,I_m}=v_{b_1,L_1}\cdots v_{b_m,L_m}$$

is the **atomic braid relation** associated with $I,a,b$.

def-author-18fc5d9b80f3-category-divisib.title: Divisibility and atomicity in a category

statement.heading: Definition
statement.source_excerpt:
Write $fg$ for the composite obtained by first traversing $f$ and then $g$. An arrow $f$ left-divides $h$ when $h=fg$ for some arrow $g$; it right-divides $h$ when $h=gf$ for some $g$. A category is cancellative when $fg=fh$ implies $g=h$ and $gf=hf$ implies $g=h$, whenever the displayed composites are defined. An atom is a nonidentity arrow which is not a composite of two nonidentity arrows. The category is atomic if, for each arrow $h$, the lengths of factorizations of $h$ into nonidentity arrows are bounded by an integer depending on $h$.

For an object $x$, the outgoing divisibility relation is left divisibility on arrows with source $x$; the incoming divisibility relation is right divisibility on arrows with target $x$. Partial-order and lattice terminology is used here only when the relevant collection of arrows is a set. When these relations are partial orders, their joins are least common multiples and their meets are greatest common divisors for the respective divisibilities. A lattice is a partially ordered set in which every pair has a meet and a join.

def-author-18fc5d9b80f3-garside-groupoid.title: Groupoid completion and Garside groupoids

statement.heading: Definition
statement.source_excerpt: For a small category $\mathcal C$, form a directed graph with its objects as vertices, one edge $[f]:x\to y$ for each arrow $f:x\to y$, and a formal reverse edge $[f]^{-1}:y\to x$. Take finite directed paths and identify paths by the smallest equivalence relation compatible with concatenation containing $[1_x]=1_x$, $[f][g]=[fg]$ for composable arrows, and $[f][f]^{-1}=1_x$, $[f]^{-1}[f]=1_y$. The resulting category is the groupoid completion of $\mathcal C$. A Garside groupoid is a groupoid isomorphic to the completion of a Garside category. In the one-object case the completion is a group, called the group of fractions of that categorical Garside monoid.

def-author-5a1e77100001-salvetti-poset.title: The incident facet and chamber poset

statement.heading: Definition
statement.source_excerpt: For the facets, incidence and localized chambers of *Facet incidence and localized chamber signs*, define $P(\mathcal A)=\{(F,C):F\in\mathcal F,\ C\in\mathcal C,\ F\preceq C\}$. Give it the relation $(F,C)\leq(G,D)$ if $F\preceq G$ and $C_F\subseteq D_G$. A partial order has the reflexivity, antisymmetry and transitivity axioms of *Partial order and partially ordered set*. This is Paris's $\operatorname{Sal}_0(\mathcal A)$, with the same direction of ordering.

source_references.title: Luis Paris, K(π, 1) conjecture for Artin groups (2014)

def-author-5f10a31d9e26-complete-local-f.title: Complete-local smooth threefold flops and their slice data

statement.heading: Definition
statement.source_excerpt:
Work over $\mathbb C$, with the Axiom of Choice. All schemes below are integral Noetherian schemes. In this complete-local setting, nonsingular (the authors' smooth-source convention) means that every local ring is regular: its Krull dimension equals the minimal number of generators of its maximal ideal. The Krull dimension of a nonzero commutative ring is the supremum of the lengths of its strict chains of prime ideals, where length counts strict inclusions. Projective means admitting a closed immersion into some finite-dimensional projective space over the base. A resolution of a normal scheme is such a projective morphism from a nonsingular scheme, isomorphic over the nonsingular locus; in particular it is birational. A partial resolution permits a normal singular source, retaining projectivity and this isomorphism condition. Its exceptional locus is the locus where the morphism is not an isomorphism.

A complete-local Du Val surface singularity means $\mathbb C\llbracket a,b,c\rrbracket/(q)$, up to formal change of coordinates, with $q$ one of
$$A_r:a^2+b^2+c^{r+1}\ (r\geq1),\quad D_r:a^2+b^2c+c^{r-1}\ (r\geq4),\quad E_6:a^2+b^3+c^4,\quad E_7:a^2+b^3+bc^3,\quad E_8:a^2+b^3+c^5.$$
Its minimal resolution $\pi:Y_{\min}\to S$ is the resolution through which every resolution of $S$ factors over $S$. Its exceptional curves are the reduced irreducible components $E_i$ of $\pi^{-1}(0)$, each isomorphic to $\mathbb P^1$ with $E_i^2=-2$. Their dual graph has one vertex per $E_i$ and an edge for each intersection of distinct curves; it is the corresponding finite ADE diagram. These existence and configuration facts are imported below.

A complete-local isolated compound Du Val (cDV) singularity here is a three-dimensional isolated hypersurface singularity $R=\mathbb C\llbracket u,v,x,y\rrbracket/(F)$ whose sufficiently general hyperplane section $R/(g)$ is a Du Val surface singularity. Fix a projective crepant resolution $f:X\to\operatorname{Spec}R$ whose exceptional locus is a nonempty union of curves and which is an isomorphism away from the closed point. Here crepant means $K_X=f^*K_{\operatorname{Spec}R}$, with compatible canonical divisors; equivalently the canonical (dualizing) sheaves satisfy $\omega_X\cong f^*\omega_R$, compatibly over the isomorphism locus. This is the complete-local smooth flopping setting used below.

Choose a sufficiently general section $g$ for which $Y=X\times_{\operatorname{Spec}R}\operatorname{Spec}(R/(g))$ is a partial crepant resolution of $S=\operatorname{Spec}(R/(g))$. The minimal resolution factors as $Y_{\min}\xrightarrow{h}Y\to S$. Write $\Delta$ for its finite ADE diagram and $J\subseteq\Delta$ for precisely the vertices $i$ whose curve $E_i$ is mapped to a point by $h$. The images of the remaining curves are the exceptional curves of $Y\to S$, corresponding to those of $f$; write $n=|\Delta\setminus J|$. Here exceptional curves of $f$ are the reduced one-dimensional irreducible components of its closed fibre.

For a unital ring $B$ and a left $B$-module $U$, a projective resolution is an exact augmented complex $\cdots\to P_1\to P_0\to U\to0$ with projective terms. Its length is at most $d$ when $P_j=0$ for $j>d$. Set $\operatorname{pd}_B U=\inf\{d\geq0:U\text{ has such a resolution of length at most }d\}$, with value $\infty$ when no finite length occurs. Supply projective resolutions for the modules under consideration and define
$$\operatorname{Ext}_B^q(U,V)=H^q\operatorname{Hom}_B(P_\bullet(U),V)\quad(q\geq0),\qquad d^q(f)=f\circ d_{q+1}.$$
These resolutions exist under our Axiom of Choice, and the comparison with derived-category morphisms identifies the resulting Ext groups canonically for different supplied resolutions. Right $B$-modules use these same constructions as left $B^{\mathrm{op}}$-modules. Thus global dimension below takes the supremum of $\operatorname{pd}$ over all right modules, without restricting to finite modules.

An NCCR in this three-dimensional setting is an algebra $\Lambda=\operatorname{End}_R M$, where $M$ is a finitely generated reflexive $R$-module, $\Lambda$ is maximal Cohen--Macaulay over $R$, and $\operatorname{gl.dim}\Lambda=3$. Reflexive means that the evaluation map $M\to\operatorname{Hom}_R(\operatorname{Hom}_R(M,R),R)$ is an isomorphism; maximal Cohen--Macaulay means $\operatorname{depth}_R\Lambda=\dim R=3$, where $\operatorname{depth}_R L=\inf\{i\geq0:\operatorname{Ext}^i_R(R/\mathfrak m,L)\ne0\}$ and $\mathfrak m$ is the maximal ideal; global dimension is the supremum of projective dimensions of right modules.

For an $\mathcal O_X$-module sheaf $\mathcal F$, let $\mathcal F_{\mathrm{ab}}$ be its underlying abelian sheaf. Under our Axiom of Choice, fix the functorial injective-resolution datum on abelian sheaves supplied by the sheaf-cohomology definition cited below. Write $0\to\mathcal F_{\mathrm{ab}}\to\mathcal I^0(\mathcal F_{\mathrm{ab}})\to\mathcal I^1(\mathcal F_{\mathrm{ab}})\to\cdots$ for its resolution and $\mathcal I^\bullet(\mathcal F_{\mathrm{ab}})$ for the deleted complex. Define
$$H^q(X,\mathcal F)=H^q\bigl(\Gamma(X,\mathcal I^\bullet(\mathcal F_{\mathrm{ab}}))\bigr)\quad(q\geq0).$$
Here $\Gamma(X,-)$ is global sections and the right-hand $H^q$ is cochain cohomology. For $a\in R$, multiplication through the structure morphism $f$ gives an abelian-sheaf endomorphism $\mu_a$ of $\mathcal F_{\mathrm{ab}}$; set $a\cdot\xi=H^q(X,\mu_a)(\xi)$. This defines the $R$-module structure used below, independently of the resolution datum up to canonical $R$-linear isomorphism. In degree zero this identifies $H^0(X,\mathcal F)$ with $\Gamma(X,\mathcal F)$. In particular $H^1(X,\mathcal L_i^{-1})$ below is sheaf cohomology with this $R$-action; its finite generation and the associated bundle extension remain part of the cited geometric construction.

For the arrangement statements fix the following basic Van den Bergh choice, rather than an arbitrary NCCR. Put $I=\Delta\setminus J$ and label the exceptional curves of $f$ by $C_i$ for $i\in I$. Choose line bundles $\mathcal L_i$ with $\deg(\mathcal L_i|_{C_k})=\delta_{ik}$. Let $m_i=r_i-1$ be the minimal number of $R$-generators of $H^1(X,\mathcal L_i^{-1})$. Choose an ordered minimal generating set $(\xi_{i1},\ldots,\xi_{im_i})$ of this $R$-module and take the bundle extension associated to this chosen generating set by the Van den Bergh construction recorded in External input:
$$0\longrightarrow\mathcal O_X^{\oplus(r_i-1)}\longrightarrow\mathcal E_i\longrightarrow\mathcal L_i\longrightarrow0.$$
Set $\mathcal V=\mathcal O_X\oplus\bigoplus_{i\in I}\mathcal E_i$ and $\mathcal T=\mathcal V^\vee$, where $(-)^\vee=\mathcal Hom_{\mathcal O_X}(-,\mathcal O_X)$. These are basic tilting bundles: their indecomposable summands are pairwise nonisomorphic and occur once; each bundle has vanishing positive self-Ext, and its derived Hom detects zero objects of $D^b(\operatorname{coh}X)$. The bundle $\mathcal V$ is generated by global sections. The existence and stated properties are imported below. We use usual function composition for endomorphism multiplication and fix
$$M=H^0(X,\mathcal V)=R\oplus\bigoplus_{i\in I}M_i,\qquad\Lambda=\operatorname{End}_R M\cong\operatorname{End}_X\mathcal V,\qquad A=\operatorname{End}_X\mathcal T\cong\operatorname{End}_R H^0(X,\mathcal T).$$
Here $M_i=H^0(X,\mathcal E_i)$, $\operatorname{rank}_R M_i=r_i>0$, and $r_0=1$ labels the free summand. The pushdown $M$ is basic and $\Lambda$ is an NCCR. This is the globally generated bundle choice in Hirano--Wemyss Setup 4.1; Wemyss Notation 2.10 uses $\mathcal T$ as $\mathcal V_X$.

For either $\Gamma=A$ or $\Gamma=\Lambda$, write $e_0,(e_i)_{i\in I}$ for the summand projections and $r=(1,(r_i)_{i\in I})$. The rank-vector real stability space is
$$\Theta_r(\Gamma)=\{\theta\in\mathbb R^{\{0\}\cup I}:\theta_0+\sum_{i\in I}r_i\theta_i=0\}.$$
For a finite-dimensional right $\Gamma$-module $Q$, its dimension vector has entries $\dim_{\mathbb C}Qe_i$, and $\theta(Q)=\sum_i\theta_i\dim_{\mathbb C}Qe_i$. A module $Q$ of dimension vector $r$ is $\theta$-semistable when $\theta(N)\geq0$ for every submodule $N\subseteq Q$, and stable when this is strict for every nonzero proper submodule. A weight is generic when all its semistable modules of dimension vector $r$ are stable. The real chamber convention is specified in the next paragraph. The independent curve coordinates are $(\theta_i)_{i\in I}$; $\theta_0=-\sum_{i\in I}r_i\theta_i$. No assertion for all dimension vectors or for an arbitrary NCCR is intended.

Put $W_r(\Gamma)=\{\theta\in\Theta_r(\Gamma):\text{some dimension-}r\text{ module is semistable but not stable}\}$. This is the wall locus. A GIT chamber is a connected component, in the real Euclidean topology, of $\Theta_r(\Gamma)\setminus W_r(\Gamma)$. Precisely, a wall hyperplane is a codimension-one linear subspace $H$ of $\Theta_r(\Gamma)$ for which there exist $\theta\in H$ and an open ball $B$ about $\theta$ with $W_r(\Gamma)\cap B=H\cap B$. A wall face in $H$ is a connected component of the set of such points $\theta$; two distinct chambers are adjacent when their closures contain the same wall face. Thus the hyperplane and its open wall faces are distinguished. These conventions use the actual nongeneric locus, rather than every possible submodule-dimension hyperplane. On rational weights they use Wemyss's rank-vector GIT convention; their continuation to real weights by the same inequalities is justified below.

Let $\operatorname{coh}X$ be the category of coherent $\mathcal O_X$-modules and $\operatorname{mod}\Lambda$ the category of finitely generated right $\Lambda$-modules, with their usual module morphisms. For these essentially small abelian categories we use small equivalent models. Write $D^b(\operatorname{coh}X)$ and $D^b(\operatorname{mod}\Lambda)$ for the localizations of their bounded cochain homotopy categories at quasi-isomorphisms, with the cochain shift and distinguished cone triangles. Exact functors are additive functors equipped with a shift isomorphism and preserving distinguished triangles. A natural isomorphism is an invertible natural transformation; $\operatorname{Auteq}$ denotes exact autoequivalences modulo natural isomorphism. The size condition and abelian-category hypotheses are justified below.

For the tilting assertions, view a bounded coherent complex $K$ as a complex in the abelian category $\operatorname{Mod}(\mathcal O_X)$ of all $\mathcal O_X$-module sheaves, using the exact inclusion of coherent sheaves. For a finite locally free sheaf $E$ in degree zero, choose a bounded-below injective replacement $K\to I_K^\bullet$ in this ambient category and put
$$\mathbf R\operatorname{Hom}_X(E,K)=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal O_X}(E,I_K^\bullet)\in D^+(\mathbf{Ab}),\qquad\operatorname{Ext}_X^p(E,F)=H^p\mathbf R\operatorname{Hom}_X(E,F)\quad(p\geq0)$$
for a coherent sheaf $F$ in degree zero. Here $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal O_X}$ means global sheaf morphisms, and the complex differential is postcomposition with $d_I$. The resolution construction is independent up to natural isomorphism. These are global Ext groups and global derived Hom. In particular, positive self-Ext vanishing for $E$ means $\operatorname{Ext}_X^p(E,E)=0$ for every $p>0$; detection of zero means that $\mathbf R\operatorname{Hom}_X(E,K)\cong0$ implies $K\cong0$ in $D^b(\operatorname{coh}X)$. Apply these conventions to each of $\mathcal V$ and $\mathcal T$. Injectives are taken in $\operatorname{Mod}(\mathcal O_X)$; their existence and the replacement hypotheses are checked below.

Thus global dimension below takes the supremum of $\operatorname{pd}$ over all right modules, without restricting to finite modules.

An NCCR in this three-dimensional setting is an algebra $\Lambda=\operatorname{End}_R M$, where $M$ is a finitely generated reflexive $R$-module, $\Lambda$ is maximal Cohen--Macaulay over $R$, and $\operatorname{gl.dim}\Lambda=3$. Reflexive means that the evaluation map $M\to\operatorname{Hom}_R(\operatorname{Hom}_R(M,R),R)$ is an isomorphism; maximal Cohen--Macaulay means $\operatorname{depth}_R\Lambda=\dim R=3$, where $\operatorname{depth}_R L=\inf\{i\geq0:\operatorname{Ext}^i_R(R/\mathfrak m,L)\ne0\}$ and $\mathfrak m$ is the maximal ideal; global dimension is the supremum of projective dimensions of right modules.

For an $\mathcal O_X$-module sheaf $\mathcal F$, let $\mathcal F_{\mathrm{ab}}$ be its underlying abelian sheaf. Under our Axiom of Choice, fix the functorial injective-resolution datum on abelian sheaves supplied by the sheaf-cohomology definition cited below. $$\Theta_r(\Gamma)=\{\theta\in\mathbb R^{\{0\}\cup I}:\theta_0+\sum_{i\in I}r_i\theta_i=0\}.$$
For a finite-dimensional right $\Gamma$-module $Q$, its dimension vector has entries $\dim_{\mathbb C}Qe_i$, and $\theta(Q)=\sum_i\theta_i\dim_{\mathbb C}Qe_i$. A module $Q$ of dimension vector $r$ is $\theta$-semistable when $\theta(N)\geq0$ for every submodule $N\subseteq Q$, and stable when this is strict for every nonzero proper submodule. def-brink-howlett-artin-tits-normalisers.title: Brink–Howlett groupoid

statement.heading: Definition
statement.source_excerpt:
Let $\Gamma$ be a Coxeter diagram with vertex set $\Gamma_0$, Coxeter group $W$ with simple generators $s_i$, and geometric representation on the real vector space with basis $(\alpha_i)_{i\in\Gamma_0}$. Fix $J\subseteq\Gamma_0$. For $I\subseteq\Gamma_0$ write $W_I=\langle s_i:i\in I\rangle$; an associate of $J$ is a subset $I$ for which $W_I$ is conjugate to $W_J$ in $W$.

The **Brink–Howlett groupoid** $\mathcal{BH}(J)$ has the associates of $J$ as objects. For associates $I,K$, its morphisms $I\to K$ are tagged by their source and target and have labels

$$\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{BH}(J)}(I,K)=\{x\in W:\{\alpha_i:i\in I\}=\{x\alpha_k:k\in K\}\}.$$

For $x:I\to K$ and $y:K\to L$, their left-to-right composite is $xy:I\to L$. The identity at $I$ has label $1\in W$.

def-chamber-labels-artin-tits-normaliser.title: Algebraic chamber-label set

statement.heading: Definition
statement.source_excerpt:
Let $(W,S)$ be a Coxeter system with $S=\{s_i:i\in\Gamma_0\}$, where the index set $\Gamma_0$ may be infinite. Let $\ell(w)$ be the least number of simple generators in a word representing $w\in W$. For $K\subseteq\Gamma_0$, let $W_K=\langle s_k:k\in K\rangle$ be the standard parabolic subgroup generated by those simple generators. Fix $J\subseteq\Gamma_0$.

The **algebraic chamber-label set** is $\mathrm{Cham}(J)=\{(x,I)\in W\times\mathcal P(\Gamma_0): W_Jx=xW_I\text{ and }\ell(x)\leq\ell(xu)\text{ for every }u\in W_I\}$. Here $\mathcal P(\Gamma_0)$ is the set of all subsets of $\Gamma_0$, and $W_Jx=\{vx:v\in W_J\}$ and $xW_I=\{xu:u\in W_I\}$. Thus the length condition says that $x$ has minimal length in the coset $xW_I$.

def-chamber-open-sets-artin-tits-normali.title: Chamber open sets used for the topological equivalence

statement.heading: Definition
statement.source_excerpt:
Let $(W,S)$ be a Coxeter system with finite $W$, and let $J\subseteq S$. Use the finite-dimensional relative space $E=\Theta_J$, its finite set $\mathcal H^J$ of distinct linear hyperplanes, and the relative complexified complement $\mathcal X_J^{\mathbb C}$ from [def-relative-complement-artin-tits-normalisers](item-def-relative-complement-artin-tits-normalisers). Thus $\mathcal X_J^{\mathbb C}$ consists of $x+iy$ with $x,y\in E$ and no $H\in\mathcal H^J$ containing both $x$ and $y$. The arrangement has ambient domain $E$; its chambers are the connected components of $E\setminus\bigcup_{H\in\mathcal H^J}H$, and adjacent chambers are distinct chambers sharing a wall, as in [def-chambers-walls-artin-tits-normalisers](item-def-chambers-walls-artin-tits-normalisers).

For $H\in\mathcal H^J$ and a chamber $C$, let $D_H(C)$ be the open half-space bounded by $H$ that contains $C$: if $a:E\to\mathbb R$ is a nonzero linear functional with kernel $H$, it is either $\{v:a(v)>0\}$ or $\{v:a(v)<0\}$, according to which contains $C$. Define

$$X_C=\{x+iy\in\mathcal X_J^{\mathbb C}:\text{ for every }H\in\mathcal H^J,\ x\in H\Rightarrow y\in D_H(C)\}.$$

Let $C,C'$ be adjacent, and let $H_0$ be their unique separating hyperplane. Define

$$X_{C,C'}=\{x+iy\in\mathcal X_J^{\mathbb C}:x\in D_{H_0}(C),\ \text{and for every }H\in\mathcal H^J,\ x\in H\Rightarrow y\in D_H(C)\cap D_H(C')\}.$$

Define $X_{C',C}$ by interchanging $C$ and $C'$ in this formula. These are subsets of $\mathcal X_J^{\mathbb C}$ with its subspace topology.

def-chamber-paths-artin-tits-normalisers.title: Chamber paths, concatenation and wall words

statement.heading: Definition
statement.source_excerpt:
Work in the finite-rank relative chamber arrangement with fixed $J\subseteq\Gamma_0$ and Coxeter group $W$ of the adjacent-wall formula. Its chambers are labelled by pairs $(x,I)\in\mathrm{Cham}(J)$: $W_Jx=xW_I$ and $x$ has minimum word length in $xW_I$. A chamber is a connected component of the arrangement complement; two distinct chambers are adjacent when they share a wall, meaning a codimension-one intersection of a chamber closure with an arrangement hyperplane.

A **path** is a finite nonempty sequence $p=((x_1,I_1),\ldots,(x_m,I_m))$ of chamber labels such that each consecutive pair labels adjacent chambers. Its source is $s(p)=(x_1,I_1)$, its target is $t(p)=(x_m,I_m)$, and its length is $m-1$. If $q=((y_1,K_1),\ldots,(y_n,K_n))$ and $t(p)=s(q)$, their **concatenation** is $p*q=((x_1,I_1),\ldots,(x_m,I_m),(y_2,K_2),\ldots,(y_n,K_n))$.

For each consecutive pair, let $a_i\in\Gamma_0\setminus I_i$ be the index supplied by the adjacent-wall formula, so that $\omega_{a_i,I_i}(x_i,I_i)=(x_{i+1},I_{i+1})$. The length-one path consisting of this pair is called a **simple wall crossing**, and is denoted $\omega_{a_i,I_i}:(x_i,I_i)\to(x_{i+1},I_{i+1})$. Thus $p$ is the ordered concatenation of its simple wall crossings when $m>1$. Define its **wall word element** by $v_p=v_{a_1,I_1}\cdots v_{a_{m-1},I_{m-1}}\in W$, where each $v_{a_i,I_i}$ is the simple wall-crossing element. When $m=1$, the empty product is the identity of $W$.

def-chambers-walls-artin-tits-normaliser.title: Chambers, walls and adjacency

statement.heading: Definition
statement.source_excerpt:
Let $(T,\mathcal H)$ be a hyperplane arrangement in a finite-dimensional real vector space $E$ with its Euclidean topology, as in [def-hyperplane-arrangement-artin-tits-normalisers](item-def-hyperplane-arrangement-artin-tits-normalisers) and [def-arrangement-topology-interface-artin-tits-prerequisites](item-def-arrangement-topology-interface-artin-tits-prerequisites). Thus $T$ is convex and each member of $\mathcal H$ is a linear hyperplane meeting $T$. Give the complement $T\setminus\bigcup_{H\in\mathcal H}H$ its subspace topology. Its connected components are the **chambers** of the arrangement.

For a chamber $C$, let $\overline C$ be its closure in $E$: the set of points every open neighbourhood of which meets $C$. The affine hull of a nonempty set is its smallest containing affine subspace, and its affine dimension is the dimension of that hull. A **wall** of $C$ is an intersection $\overline C\cap H$, for $H\in\mathcal H$, whose affine dimension is one less than the affine dimension of $C$. Two distinct chambers are **adjacent** if they share a wall. The wall is the intersection itself; the hyperplane $H$ is its supporting hyperplane and is not the wall by this convention.

def-classical-complement-artin-tits-norm.title: Classical complexified hyperplane complement

statement.heading: Definition
statement.source_excerpt:
Let $(W,S)$ be a Coxeter system with $S$ finite. Use the finite-dimensional real dual space $\Theta$, its topology, the Tits cone $\mathrm{Cone}$ and its interior $\mathrm{Cone}^{\circ}$, and the set $\mathcal H$ of distinct reflecting hyperplanes from [def-coxeter-arrangement-artin-tits-normalisers](item-def-coxeter-arrangement-artin-tits-normalisers). The classical complexified hyperplane complement is

$$\mathcal X^{\mathbb C}=(\mathrm{Cone}^{\circ}\times\mathrm{Cone}^{\circ})\setminus\bigcup_{H\in\mathcal H}(H\times H).$$

It has the subspace topology inherited from the product topology on $\mathrm{Cone}^{\circ}\times\mathrm{Cone}^{\circ}$. In particular, a point $(x,y)$ belongs to $\mathcal X^{\mathbb C}$ exactly when $x,y\in\mathrm{Cone}^{\circ}$ and no reflecting hyperplane contains both $x$ and $y$.

When $W$ is finite, identify $(x,y)\in\Theta\times\Theta$ with $x\otimes 1+y\otimes i\in\Theta\otimes_{\mathbb R}\mathbb C$. Under this identification,

$$\mathcal X^{\mathbb C}=(\Theta\otimes_{\mathbb R}\mathbb C)\setminus\bigcup_{H\in\mathcal H}(H\otimes_{\mathbb R}\mathbb C).$$

Here $H\otimes_{\mathbb R}\mathbb C$ denotes the complexification of the real hyperplane $H$, viewed as a subspace of the complexification of $\Theta$.

def-codimension-two-artin-tits-normalise.title: Codimension-two relations

statement.heading: Definition
statement.source_excerpt:
Let $(W,S)$ be a finite-rank Coxeter system with diagram vertex set $\Gamma_0$ and geometric roots $\Phi$. For $L\subseteq\Gamma_0$, let $W_L$ be the subgroup generated by the simple reflections indexed by $L$, and put $\Phi_L=\{w\alpha_i:w\in W_L,\ i\in L\}$. Fix $J\subseteq\Gamma_0$ and a relative chamber label $(x,I)\in\mathrm{Cham}(J)$, meaning that $W_Jx=xW_I$ and $x$ has minimum length in $xW_I$.

A chamber path in the relative arrangement $(\mathrm{Cone}(J)^\circ,\mathcal H^J)$ is a finite nonempty sequence of chambers with consecutive chambers adjacent; its length is the number of successive pairs. It is **geodesic** when its length is minimal among chamber paths with the same endpoints. For an eligible vertex $a\notin I$, write $\omega_{a,I}$ for the simple wall crossing at $(x,I)$ as defined in [def-simple-wall-crossing-artin-tits-normalisers](item-def-simple-wall-crossing-artin-tits-normalisers).

Choose distinct $a,b\in\Gamma_0\setminus I$ such that $|\Phi_{I\cup\{a,b\}}\setminus\Phi_I|<\infty$. Let $q=v_{a,b,I}:I\to K$ be the two-generator element of [lem-two-generator-minimal-artin-tits-normalisers](item-lem-two-generator-minimal-artin-tits-normalisers). The two-geodesic lemma supplies exactly two geodesic paths $p_a,p_b$ from $(x,I)$ to $(xq,K)$, beginning respectively with $\omega_{a,I}$ and $\omega_{b,I}$. The formal relation $p_a=p_b$ identifying these paths is called a **codimension-two relation**.

def-complement-interface-artin-tits-prer.title: Complexified complements in an open convex cone

statement.heading: Definition
statement.source_excerpt:
Let $E$ be a finite-dimensional real vector space with the Euclidean topology supplied by linear coordinates. Let $T\subseteq E$ be nonempty, open and convex, and let $\mathcal A$ be a locally finite arrangement in $T$: its members are linear hyperplanes meeting $T$, and every point of $T$ has a neighbourhood meeting only finitely many members. Define the complement

$$M(T,\mathcal A)=(T\times T)\setminus\bigcup_{H\in\mathcal A}(H\times H).$$

Give $T\times T$ the product topology and $M(T,\mathcal A)$ its subspace topology: its open sets are intersections of $M(T,\mathcal A)$ with open subsets of $T\times T$.

When $T=E$, put $E_{\mathbb C}=\mathbb C\otimes_{\mathbb R}E$ and identify $(x,y)$ with $1\otimes x+i\otimes y$, also written $x+iy$. For each $H\in\mathcal A$, its complexification inside $E_{\mathbb C}$ means $H_{\mathbb C}=\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb C}\{1\otimes h:h\in H\}$. Under this identification the complement is $E_{\mathbb C}\setminus\bigcup_{H\in\mathcal A}H_{\mathbb C}$.

Suppose a group $G$ acts on $E$ by invertible real-linear maps and each $g\in G$ preserves $T$ and permutes $\mathcal A$. The action convention is $ex=x$ and $(gh)x=g(hx)$. The diagonal action on $T\times T$ is $g\cdot(x,y)=(gx,gy)$; its restriction to the complement is the diagonal action on $M(T,\mathcal A)$.

A homeomorphism is a continuous bijection with continuous inverse. A covering-space action is an action by homeomorphisms for which every point has an open neighbourhood $U$ satisfying $gU\cap U=\varnothing$ for every nonidentity $g$. Setwise preservation alone does not assert this condition or path connectedness. Path connectedness means that for any $p,q\in M(T,\mathcal A)$ there is a continuous map $\gamma:[0,1]\to M(T,\mathcal A)$ with $\gamma(0)=p$ and $\gamma(1)=q$, where $[0,1]$ has its usual subspace topology from $\mathbb R$.

def-connected-support-artin-tits-normali.title: Connected component notation [I,a]

statement.heading: Definition
statement.source_excerpt:
Let $\Gamma$ be a Coxeter diagram with vertex set $\Gamma_0$, let $I\subseteq\Gamma_0$, and let $a\in I^c=\Gamma_0\setminus I$. As in [def-set-notation-artin-tits-normalisers](item-def-set-notation-artin-tits-normalisers), put $I+a=I\cup\{a\}$. Write $\Gamma(I+a)$ for the induced subgraph of $\Gamma$ on $I+a$: its vertices are exactly those in $I+a$, and it contains exactly the edges of $\Gamma$ whose endpoints both lie in $I+a$, with their labels retained.

The notation $[I,a]$ denotes the vertex set of the connected component of $\Gamma(I+a)$ containing $a$. Explicitly, $[I,a]$ consists of the vertices $v\in I+a$ for which a path in $\Gamma(I+a)$ has endpoints $a$ and $v$; a path of length zero is allowed. In particular, $a\in[I,a]\subseteq I+a$.

def-core-atomic-cosets-artin-tits-normal.title: Core and atomic double cosets

statement.heading: Definition
statement.source_excerpt:
Let $(W,S)$ be a Coxeter system with $S=\{s_i:i\in\Gamma_0\}$. For $J\subseteq\Gamma_0$, let $W_J=\langle s_j:j\in J\rangle$ be its standard parabolic subgroup. For $I,K\subseteq\Gamma_0$ and $x\in W$, the $(I,K)$-double coset of $x$ is the set $W_IxW_K=\{uxv:u\in W_I,\ v\in W_K\}$. The set $W_Ix=\{ux:u\in W_I\}$ is the right coset of $W_I$ represented by $x$, and $xW_K=\{xv:v\in W_K\}$ is the left coset of $W_K$ represented by $x$.

The $(I,K)$-double coset $W_IxW_K$ is **core** if $W_Ix=W_IxW_K=xW_K$ as sets. No finiteness condition is imposed on $W_I$ or $W_K$ in this definition.

For $L\subseteq\Gamma_0$ with $W_L$ finite, write $w_L$ for its unique longest element, meaning the element of maximal Coxeter length in $W_L$. For $a,a'\in L$, write $L-a=L\setminus\{a\}$ and $L-a'=L\setminus\{a'\}$. An **atomic double coset**, or **atom**, is a core double coset of the form $W_{L-a}w_LW_{L-a'}$ for such $L,a,a'$. The core condition is part of the definition; it is not asserted for arbitrary choices of $a,a'$.

def-coxeter-arrangement-artin-tits-norma.title: Reflecting hyperplanes, fundamental chamber and Tits cone

statement.heading: Definition
statement.source_excerpt:
For the geometry in this item, let the vertex set $\Gamma_0$ be finite. This is the finite-rank Coxeter-graph convention of Iyama–Wemyss, §§1.1–1.3; the Coxeter group $W$ may be infinite. Use the geometric representation, roots and algebraic dual $\Theta=V^*$ of [def-coxeter-data-artin-tits-normalisers](item-def-coxeter-data-artin-tits-normalisers), specialized to this finite vertex set, and the finite-rank realization of [def-real-coxeter-interface-artin-tits-prerequisites](item-def-real-coxeter-interface-artin-tits-prerequisites).

The coordinate map $\Theta\longrightarrow\mathbb R^{\Gamma_0}$, $f\longmapsto(f(\alpha_i))_{i\in\Gamma_0}$, is a linear isomorphism. Give $\Theta$ its transported Euclidean topology, as in [def-arrangement-topology-interface-artin-tits-prerequisites](item-def-arrangement-topology-interface-artin-tits-prerequisites). For a subset $A\subseteq\Theta$, its closure $\overline A$ consists of points every open neighbourhood of which meets $A$; its interior $A^\circ$ is the union of open subsets contained in $A$.

For each root $\alpha\in\Phi$ define the reflecting hyperplane and the set of distinct such hyperplanes by
$$H_\alpha=\{f\in\Theta:f(\alpha)=0\},\qquad\mathcal H=\{H_\alpha:\alpha\in\Phi\}.$$
Define the open fundamental chamber and its closure by
$$C=\{f\in\Theta:f(\alpha_i)>0\text{ for every }i\in\Gamma_0\},\qquad\overline C=\{f\in\Theta:f(\alpha_i)\geq0\text{ for every }i\in\Gamma_0\}.$$
The Tits cone and its interior in $\Theta$ are
$$\mathrm{Cone}=\bigcup_{w\in W}w\overline C,\qquad\mathrm{Cone}^\circ=\operatorname{int}_{\Theta}(\mathrm{Cone}).$$
The notation $w\overline C$ uses the contragredient action: $wf=f\circ\rho(w)^{-1}$. The family $\mathcal H$ is a set, so coincident hyperplanes are included only once.

statement.heading: Definition
statement.source_excerpt:
For the geometry in this item, let the vertex set $\Gamma_0$ be finite. This is the finite-rank Coxeter-graph convention of Iyama–Wemyss, §§1.1–1.3; the Coxeter group $W$ may be infinite. Use the geometric representation, roots and algebraic dual $\Theta=V^*$ of [[def-coxeter-data-artin-tits-normalisers]], specialized to this finite vertex set, and the finite-rank realization of [[def-real-coxeter-interface-artin-tits-prerequisites]].

The coordinate map $\Theta\longrightarrow\mathbb R^{\Gamma_0}$, $f\longmapsto(f(\alpha_i))_{i\in\Gamma_0}$, is a linear isomorphism. Give $\Theta$ its transported Euclidean topology, as in [[def-arrangement-topology-interface-artin-tits-prerequisites]]. For a subset $A\subseteq\Theta$, its closure $\overline A$ consists of points every open neighbourhood of which meets $A$; its interior $A^\circ$ is the union of open subsets contained in $A$.

For each root $\alpha\in\Phi$ define the reflecting hyperplane and the set of distinct such hyperplanes by
$$H_\alpha=\{f\in\Theta:f(\alpha)=0\},\qquad\mathcal H=\{H_\alpha:\alpha\in\Phi\}.$$
Define the open fundamental chamber and its closure by
$$C=\{f\in\Theta:f(\alpha_i)>0\text{ for every }i\in\Gamma_0\},\qquad\overline C=\{f\in\Theta:f(\alpha_i)\geq0\text{ for every }i\in\Gamma_0\}.$$
The Tits cone and its interior in $\Theta$ are
$$\mathrm{Cone}=\bigcup_{w\in W}w\overline C,\qquad\mathrm{Cone}^\circ=\operatorname{int}_{\Theta}(\mathrm{Cone}).$$
The notation $w\overline C$ uses the contragredient action: $wf=f\circ\rho(w)^{-1}$. The family $\mathcal H$ is a set, so coincident hyperplanes are included only once.

def-coxeter-data-artin-tits-normalisers.title: Coxeter-system, roots, length and weak-order conventions

statement.heading: Definition
statement.source_excerpt:
Let $S=\{s_i:i\in\Gamma_0\}$ be indexed by a set $\Gamma_0$, possibly infinite, and let $m:S\times S\to\{1,2,3,\ldots\}\cup\{\infty\}$ be symmetric, with $m(s,s)=1$ and $m(s,t)\geq 2$ for distinct $s,t$. The Coxeter diagram $\Gamma$ has vertex set $\Gamma_0$: distinct vertices $i,j$ are joined when $m(s_i,s_j)\geq3$, with the edge labelled by $m(s_i,s_j)$ when that value is at least $4$ or infinity; an unlabelled edge denotes $3$, and no edge denotes $2$. The associated Coxeter group is $W=\langle S\mid s^2=1,\ (st)^{m(s,t)}=1\text{ for }s\ne t\text{ with }m(s,t)<\infty\rangle$. The pair $(W,S)$ is its Coxeter system. The diagram is spherical, or of finite type, precisely when $W$ is finite.

Let $V=\bigoplus_{i\in\Gamma_0}\mathbb R\alpha_i$, the real vector space of finite linear combinations of the basis vectors $\alpha_i$. Define the symmetric bilinear Coxeter form $B$ by $B(\alpha_i,\alpha_i)=1$, $B(\alpha_i,\alpha_j)=-\cos(\pi/m(s_i,s_j))$ for distinct $i,j$ with finite label, and $B(\alpha_i,\alpha_j)=-1$ when that label is infinity. For $s_i\in S$ put $r_i(v)=v-2B(v,\alpha_i)\alpha_i$. The standard geometric representation is the homomorphism $\rho:W\to\mathrm{GL}(V)$ with $\rho(s_i)=r_i$; write $w v$ for $\rho(w)v$. Its roots are $\Phi=\{w\alpha_i:w\in W,\ i\in\Gamma_0\}$. Put $V_+=\{\sum_i a_i\alpha_i:a_i\geq0\}$, with finite support, and define the positive and negative roots by $\Phi^+=\Phi\cap V_+$ and $\Phi^-=-\Phi^+$.

The length $\ell(w)$ is the least number of simple generators in a word representing $w$, with the empty word representing the identity. Define the prefix weak order by $u\leq w$ when $w=ux$ for some $x\in W$ and $\ell(w)=\ell(u)+\ell(x)$. Following the article, call such a $u$ a left divisor of $w$ and call this the left weak order; the finite-rank supplier calls the same prefix convention right weak order.

Let $\Theta=V^*=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb R}(V,\mathbb R)$, the algebraic dual. Its contragredient action is $(wf)(v)=f(\rho(w)^{-1}v)$ for $w\in W$, $f\in\Theta$ and $v\in V$. No identification of $V$ with $V^*$ or nondegeneracy of $B$ is assumed.

def-d4-example-data-artin-tits-normalise.title: D4 diagram and generator conventions

statement.heading: Definition
statement.source_excerpt:
For this example, let $\Gamma=D_4$ denote the Coxeter diagram with vertices $\{1,2,3,4\}$ and three unlabelled edges $\{1,2\}$, $\{2,3\}$ and $\{2,4\}$. Thus vertex $2$ is trivalent: it is incident to exactly three edges. Equivalently, the Coxeter matrix has $m(s_i,s_i)=1$, $m(s_2,s_i)=m(s_i,s_2)=3$ for $i\in\{1,3,4\}$, and $m(s_i,s_j)=2$ for distinct $i,j\in\{1,3,4\}$.

Let $(W,S)$ be the associated Coxeter system, with $S=\{s_1,s_2,s_3,s_4\}$, and set $J=\{2\}$. Write $s=s_1$, $t=s_2$, $u=s_3$ and $v=s_4$; in particular $t$ is the simple reflection at the trivalent vertex.

Let $V=\bigoplus_{i=1}^4\mathbb R\alpha_i$ be the standard geometric representation: its Coxeter form satisfies $B(\alpha_i,\alpha_i)=1$, $B(\alpha_2,\alpha_i)=-1/2$ for $i\in\{1,3,4\}$, and $B(\alpha_i,\alpha_j)=0$ for distinct $i,j\in\{1,3,4\}$; the generator $s_i$ acts by $x\mapsto x-2B(x,\alpha_i)\alpha_i$. Let $\Theta=V^*$ be the space of real linear functionals on $V$, with the contragredient action $(wf)(x)=f(w^{-1}x)$ for $w\in W$, $f\in\Theta$ and $x\in V$.

def-deligne-ribbon-mapping-artin-tits-no.title: Assignment from wall crossings to ribbon generators

statement.heading: Definition
statement.source_excerpt:
Let $\Gamma$ be a finite-rank spherical Coxeter diagram, meaning that its Coxeter group $W$ is finite, with vertex set $\Gamma_0$, and fix $J\subseteq\Gamma_0$. For $I\subseteq\Gamma_0$, write $W_I$ for the subgroup generated by the simple reflections indexed by $I$. A chamber label is a pair $(x,I)$ with $W_Jx=xW_I$ and $x$ of minimum Coxeter length in $xW_I$. Identify these labels with the chambers of the relative arrangement. Let $\mathcal D=\mathcal D(J)$ be its arrangement groupoid: its objects are the chambers, its directed generating arrows are the simple crossings between adjacent chambers, and its positive-category relations identify geodesic paths with common endpoints. Let $\mathcal R=\mathcal R(J)$ be the reduced ribbon groupoid, whose objects are the subsets $I$ for which $W_I$ is conjugate to $W_J$ and whose elementary arrows are the ribbons $\mu_{a,I}$ for $a\in\Gamma_0\setminus I$.

Define $\mathcal G$ on the directed chamber graph by $\mathcal G(x,I)=I$ on vertices and $\mathcal G(\omega_{a,I})=\mu_{a,I}$ on a generating arrow $\omega_{a,I}:(x,I)\to(y,K)$. Explicitly, with $T=I\cup\{a\}$, the target is $K=T\setminus\{\iota_T(a)\}$, where $\iota_T$ is the opposition permutation of the finite parabolic $W_T$. The elementary ribbon is $\mu_{a,I}=\Delta_I^{-1}\Delta_T:I\to K$, where $\Delta_L$ is the positive reduced-word lift of the longest element of $W_L$.

Let $N(W,J)=\operatorname{Norm}_W(W_J)/W_J$ act on $\mathcal D$ through its action on relative chambers. Write $\mathcal Q:\mathcal D\to\mathcal D/N(W,J)$ for the quotient functor: it sends each object and arrow to its orbit under this action. Composition is read from left to right.

def-garside-interface-artin-tits-prerequ.title: Categorical Garside structures and simple arrows

statement.heading: Definition
statement.source_excerpt:
Let $\mathcal C$ be a small category, meaning that its objects and arrows form sets. An automorphism of $\mathcal C$ means a functor $\phi:\mathcal C\to\mathcal C$ admitting a functor $\psi:\mathcal C\to\mathcal C$ with $\psi\circ\phi=\operatorname{id}_{\mathcal C}=\phi\circ\psi$ as equalities on objects and arrows. Let $\phi$ be such an automorphism, and let $\Delta$ be a natural transformation from the identity functor to $\phi$. Thus its component at $x$ is an arrow $\Delta_x:x\to\phi(x)$, and for every $f:x\to y$ one has $f\Delta_y=\Delta_x\phi(f)$ in traversal order. An arrow $f:x\to y$ is simple for this structure if there is an arrow $g:y\to\phi(x)$ with $fg=\Delta_x$.

An atomic categorical Garside structure is such a triple $(\mathcal C,\phi,\Delta)$ in which $\mathcal C$ is atomic and cancellative, every atom is simple, and, for every object $x$, both the outgoing left-divisibility order and the incoming right-divisibility order are lattices. A Garside category means a category equipped with such a structure. In the one-object case its arrows form a Garside monoid in this categorical convention. The structure has finite type if its set of simple arrows is finite.

def-geodesic-path-artin-tits-normalisers.title: Geodesic chamber paths

statement.heading: Definition
statement.source_excerpt:
Fix a finite-rank Coxeter system and a subset $J$ of its vertex set. In the relative arrangement $(\mathrm{Cone}(J)^\circ,\mathcal H^J)$, a chamber path is a finite nonempty sequence of chambers with consecutive chambers adjacent. Its length is its number of consecutive pairs. At each adjacency the path crosses the unique relative hyperplane supporting the shared wall; repeated crossings are counted with multiplicity.

A path is **geodesic** if its length is minimal among chamber paths with the same source and target. Equivalently, it crosses each hyperplane of $\mathcal H^J$ at most once. Hyperplanes are counted as distinct sets, even when different roots define the same relative hyperplane. A one-chamber path has length zero and is geodesic.

def-groupoid-action-quotient-artin-tits-.title: Free actions and quotient groupoids

statement.heading: Definition
statement.source_excerpt:
Let $N$ be a group and let $\mathcal G$ be a connected small groupoid: its objects and arrows form sets, every arrow is invertible, and there is an arrow between every ordered pair of objects. Composition is read left to right, so $ab$ means first $a$ and then $b$.

An automorphism of $\mathcal G$ is an invertible functor from $\mathcal G$ to itself. An action of $N$ on $\mathcal G$ is a homomorphism from $N$ to the group of these automorphisms, whose multiplication is composition of functors. Write $nx$ and $na$ for the images of an object $x$ and an arrow $a$ under the automorphism assigned to $n$; thus $(nm)x=n(mx)$ and $(nm)a=n(ma)$. The action is free on objects if $nx=x$ implies $n=1$.

def-groupoid-completion-artin-tits-norma.title: Groupoid completion and its universal property

statement.heading: Definition
statement.source_excerpt:
Let $\mathcal G^+$ be a small category: its objects and morphisms form sets. A groupoid is a category in which every morphism has a two-sided inverse. Composition of consecutive arrows is read from left to right.

Form a directed graph with the objects of $\mathcal G^+$ as vertices and a tagged edge $[f]:x\to y$ for every morphism $f:x\to y$ of $\mathcal G^+$. Impose the path relations $[1_x]=1_x$ and $[f][g]=[fg]$ whenever $f:x\to y$ and $g:y\to z$ are composable; the right-hand $1_x$ is the empty path. A path is a finite composable sequence of edges. The presented category has these vertices as objects and paths modulo the smallest endpoint-preserving equivalence relation containing the displayed relations and stable under concatenation.

The **groupoid completion** $\mathcal G$ of $\mathcal G^+$ is the groupoid completion of this presented category: adjoin a separately tagged reverse edge $[f]^{-1}:y\to x$ for each edge $[f]$, and impose $[f][f]^{-1}=1_x$ and $[f]^{-1}[f]=1_y$, in addition to the preceding relations. Its arrows are the resulting equivalence classes of paths. The canonical functor $\kappa:\mathcal G^+\to\mathcal G$ is the identity on objects and sends $f$ to the class of $[f]$.

For every small groupoid $\mathcal H$ and functor $F:\mathcal G^+\to\mathcal H$, there is a unique functor $\overline F:\mathcal G\to\mathcal H$ such that $\overline F\circ\kappa=F$. Thus every such $F$ factors through $\kappa$. No connectedness of $\mathcal G^+$ or $\mathcal H$, and no faithfulness of $\kappa$, is assumed.

def-groupoid-conventions-artin-tits-norm.title: Connected small groupoids and vertex groups

statement.heading: Definition
statement.source_excerpt:
A groupoid is a category in which every morphism has a two-sided inverse. Here all groupoids are small, meaning that their objects and morphisms each form a set, and connected, meaning that they are nonempty and there is a morphism between each ordered pair of objects. Composition is read left to right: for $a:x\to y$ and $b:y\to z$, the product $ab$ means $b\circ a$.

For an object $x$ of a groupoid $\mathcal G$, the vertex group $\mathcal G_x=\operatorname{End}_{\mathcal G}(x)$ consists of the morphisms $x\to x$, with composition as multiplication and the identity morphism $1_x$ as identity. The vertex groups at any two objects are isomorphic; the isomorphism need not be canonical.

def-groupoid-cover-artin-tits-normaliser.title: Groupoid coverings, universal and normal covers

statement.heading: Definition
statement.source_excerpt:
Use the small, nonempty connected groupoids and left-to-right composition convention of [def-groupoid-conventions-artin-tits-normalisers](item-def-groupoid-conventions-artin-tits-normalisers). A functor $F:\widetilde{\mathcal G}\to\mathcal G$ assigns objects to objects and morphisms to morphisms, preserving sources, targets, identities and composition. It is a **covering** if, for every morphism $\alpha:x\to y$ of $\mathcal G$ and every object $\widetilde x$ with $F(\widetilde x)=x$, there is exactly one morphism $\widetilde\alpha$ with source $\widetilde x$ and $F(\widetilde\alpha)=\alpha$. Its target $\widetilde y$ necessarily satisfies $F(\widetilde y)=y$ and is uniquely determined by the lift. Thus a covering is precisely a functor bijective on the set of morphisms with each prescribed source.

A covering is **universal** when every vertex group upstairs is trivial, meaning it contains only its identity morphism. Equivalently, for each pair of objects $\widetilde x,\widetilde y$ upstairs, $\operatorname{Hom}_{\widetilde{\mathcal G}}(\widetilde x,\widetilde y)$ contains exactly one morphism.

A **deck transformation** of $F$ is an automorphism $\phi$ of $\widetilde{\mathcal G}$, meaning an invertible functor from it to itself, satisfying the strict equality of functors $F\circ\phi=F$. The deck transformations form a group under ordinary functor composition and act on each fibre $F^{-1}(x)$ by their object maps. The covering is **normal** if this action is transitive on one fibre: any two objects in that fibre are related by a deck transformation. Equivalently, the action is transitive on every fibre.

def-hyperplane-arrangement-artin-tits-no.title: Linear hyperplane arrangements and local finiteness

statement.heading: Definition
statement.source_excerpt:
Let $E$ be a real vector space equipped with a specified topology, and give each subset of $E$ the subspace topology: its open sets are its intersections with open subsets of $E$. In the finite-dimensional setting one may use the Euclidean topology described in the arrangement interface. A subset $T\subseteq E$ is convex when $(1-t)x+ty\in T$ for all $x,y\in T$ and $0\leq t\leq1$. A linear hyperplane is a linear subspace $H\subseteq E$ of codimension one, meaning that $E/H$ has dimension one.

A hyperplane arrangement $(T,\mathcal H)$ consists of a convex subset $T\subseteq E$ and a set $\mathcal H$ of linear hyperplanes in $E$, possibly infinite, such that $H\cap T\ne\varnothing$ for every $H\in\mathcal H$.

For a convex subset $T'\subseteq T$, the restriction to $T'$ is the arrangement $(T',\mathcal H_{T'})$, where $\mathcal H_{T'}=\{H\in\mathcal H:H\cap T'\ne\varnothing\}$. It is also denoted $(T',\mathcal H)$ when the restriction of the hyperplane set is understood.

The arrangement is locally finite if, for every $x\in T$, there is an open set $U$ in the subspace topology on $T$ with $x\in U$ such that $U$ meets only finitely many distinct members of $\mathcal H$.

def-longest-elements-artin-tits-normalis.title: Longest parabolic elements and opposition permutation

statement.heading: Definition
statement.source_excerpt:
Let $(W,S)$ be a Coxeter system with $S=\{s_i:i\in\Gamma_0\}$, length $\ell$, and simple roots $\alpha_i$ in its standard geometric representation. Let $A$ be the Artin–Tits group with generators $\sigma_i$, and for $J\subseteq\Gamma_0$ write $W_J=\langle s_j:j\in J\rangle$ and $A_J=\langle\sigma_j:j\in J\rangle$. Suppose that $W_J$ is finite.

The **longest element** $w_J$ is the unique element of $W_J$ whose $\ell$-length is maximal. Its **positive lift** is $\Delta_J=\sigma_{w_J}\in A_J$: if $w_J=s_{j_1}\cdots s_{j_r}$ is a shortest expression in simple generators, set $\sigma_{w_J}=\sigma_{j_1}\cdots\sigma_{j_r}$, with the empty product equal to the identity. The **opposition permutation** $\iota_J:J\to J$ is the unique permutation satisfying $w_J\alpha_j=-\alpha_{\iota_J(j)}$ for every $j\in J$.

def-normaliser-complement-artin-tits-nor.title: Root-permuting normaliser complement

statement.heading: Definition
statement.source_excerpt:
Let $(W,S)$ be a Coxeter system with simple generators $S=\{s_i:i\in\Gamma_0\}$ and geometric representation on the real vector space with basis $\{\alpha_i:i\in\Gamma_0\}$. The index set may be infinite. For $J\subseteq\Gamma_0$, write $W_J=\langle s_j:j\in J\rangle$ and $\operatorname{Norm}_W(W_J)=\{w\in W:wW_Jw^{-1}=W_J\}$.

The **root-permuting normaliser subgroup** $N_J$, also denoted $\mathcal{BH}_J$, is

$$N_J=\mathcal{BH}_J=\{x\in W:(\forall j\in J)(\exists j'\in J)\ x\alpha_j=\alpha_{j'}\}.$$

It is the vertex group at $J$ of the Brink–Howlett groupoid and is a subgroup of $\operatorname{Norm}_W(W_J)$.

statement.heading: Definition
statement.source_excerpt:
Let $(W,S)$ be a finite-rank Coxeter system indexed by $S=\{s_i:i\in\Gamma_0\}$, let $A$ be its Artin–Tits group, and let $P=\ker(\pi:A\to W)$ be its pure Artin–Tits group. For $J\subseteq\Gamma_0$, let $W_J=\langle s_j:j\in J\rangle$ and $A_J=\langle\sigma_j:j\in J\rangle$ be the standard parabolic subgroups; the brackets denote the subgroups generated by the displayed elements.

For $G=W$ with $G_J=W_J$, or $G=A$ with $G_J=A_J$, define the **normaliser** of $G_J$ in $G$ by $\operatorname{Norm}_G(G_J)=\{g\in G:gG_Jg^{-1}=G_J\}$. Define the normaliser quotient groups $N(W,J)=\operatorname{Norm}_W(W_J)/W_J$ and $N(A,J)=\operatorname{Norm}_A(A_J)/A_J$.

Define $N(P,J)=\{\beta A_J\in N(A,J):P\cap\beta A_J\ne\varnothing\}$. Equivalently, $N(P,J)$ is the image of $P\cap\operatorname{Norm}_A(A_J)$ under the quotient homomorphism $\operatorname{Norm}_A(A_J)\to N(A,J)$.

statement.heading: Definition
statement.source_excerpt:

For $I\subseteq\Gamma_0$, write $I^c=\Gamma_0\setminus I$. def-parabolic-subgroups-artin-tits-norma.title: Standard parabolic subgroups and parabolic roots

statement.heading: Definition
statement.source_excerpt:
Let $(W,S)$ be the Coxeter system indexed by $S=\{s_i:i\in\Gamma_0\}$, with geometric action on the simple roots $\alpha_i$, root set $\Phi$, and positive and negative root sets $\Phi^+$ and $\Phi^-$ as specified in the Coxeter-data definition. The index set may be infinite. Let $A$ be the Artin–Tits group of the same Coxeter matrix: it has generators $\sigma_i$ for $i\in\Gamma_0$ and, for each distinct $i,j$ with finite $m(s_i,s_j)$, the relation equating the two alternating words in $\sigma_i,\sigma_j$ of length $m(s_i,s_j)$, one beginning with each generator. No relation is imposed for a pair with $m(s_i,s_j)=\infty$.

For $J\subseteq\Gamma_0$, the **standard parabolic subgroup of $W$ attached to $J$** is $W_J=\langle s_j:j\in J\rangle$, and the **standard parabolic subgroup of $A$ attached to $J$** is $A_J=\langle\sigma_j:j\in J\rangle$. Here brackets denote the smallest subgroup containing the displayed elements. The associated **parabolic root set** and its positive and negative parts are $\Phi_J=\{w\alpha_j:w\in W_J,\ j\in J\}$ and $\Phi_J^{\pm}=\Phi_J\cap\Phi^{\pm}$.

def-path-localisation-interface-artin-ti.title: Path presentations, congruences and formal inverses

statement.heading: Definition
statement.source_excerpt:
A small directed graph, or quiver, $Q$ consists of a set $Q_0$ of vertices, a set $Q_1$ of directed edges, and source and target functions $s,t:Q_1\to Q_0$. Its path category $P(Q)$ has the vertices as objects and finite composable sequences of edges as arrows; the empty sequence at a vertex is its identity. Composition is concatenation, read from left to right.

A path relation is a pair of paths with the same source and target. Let $R$ be a set of path relations. A path congruence is an equivalence relation on the set of all paths that relates only paths with the same endpoints and remains valid after concatenation on either side by any composable path. Write $\equiv_R$ for the smallest path congruence containing $R$. The category presented by $(Q,R)$ is $\mathcal C=P(Q)/{\equiv_R}$: its objects are the vertices, its arrows are equivalence classes of paths, and its identities and composition are induced by empty paths and concatenation.

Form the doubled quiver $\overline Q$ by adjoining, for each edge $e:x\to y$ of $Q$, a new tagged edge $e^{-1}:y\to x$. These new edges are distinct from the original edges and from one another. Regard each relation in $R$ as a relation in $P(\overline Q)$ and add the relations $ee^{-1}=1_x$ and $e^{-1}e=1_y$ for every $e:x\to y$. The resulting presented category is the groupoid completion $\mathcal C^{\mathrm{gp}}$; the canonical functor $j:\mathcal C\to\mathcal C^{\mathrm{gp}}$ sends each path class to the class of the same path in the doubled quiver.

For every small groupoid $\mathcal G$ and functor $F:\mathcal C\to\mathcal G$, there is a unique functor $\overline F:\mathcal C^{\mathrm{gp}}\to\mathcal G$ with $\overline F\circ j=F$. Oppositely directed edges already in $Q$ remain distinct generators from the newly adjoined formal inverses, although imposed relations can identify their classes. Neither cancellation in $\mathcal C$ nor faithfulness of $j$ is assumed.

def-positive-artin-monoids-artin-tits-no.title: Positive Artin and parabolic monoids

statement.heading: Definition
statement.source_excerpt:
Let $(W,S)$ be a finite-rank Coxeter system with $S=\{s_i:i\in\Gamma_0\}$, let $A$ be its Artin–Tits group with Artin generators $\sigma_i$, and let $I\subseteq\Gamma_0$. Write $A_I$ for the standard parabolic subgroup generated by the $\sigma_i$ with $i\in I$.

A **monoid** is a set with an associative binary operation and a two-sided identity. A **submonoid** of a monoid is a subset containing the identity and closed under the operation. The **positive Artin submonoid** $A^+$ is the submonoid of $A$ generated by all its Artin generators: explicitly, it consists of all finite products $\sigma_{i_1}\cdots\sigma_{i_n}$ with $n\geq 0$ and $i_k\in\Gamma_0$. The **positive parabolic submonoid** $A_I^+$ is the submonoid of $A_I$ generated by $\{\sigma_i:i\in I\}$: explicitly, it consists of the same finite products with every $i_k\in I$. In both cases the empty product is the identity of $A$.

These definitions do not require spherical type, meaning that $W$ is finite. The article imposes spherical type in Sections 5 and 6.

def-real-coxeter-interface-artin-tits-pr.title: Real Coxeter representation and contragredient notation

statement.heading: Definition
statement.source_excerpt:
Let $S$ be a finite set and $m:S\times S\to\{1,2,3,\ldots\}\cup\{\infty\}$ a Coxeter matrix: $m(s,s)=1$ and, for $s\ne t$, $m(s,t)=m(t,s)\in\{2,3,\ldots\}\cup\{\infty\}$. Its presented Coxeter group is $W=\langle S\mid s^2=1,\ (st)^{m(s,t)}=1\text{ when }s\ne t\text{ and }m(s,t)<\infty\rangle$.

Let $V=\mathbb R^S$, the space of real-valued functions on $S$, and let $e_s$ be the function that is $1$ at $s$ and $0$ elsewhere. The Coxeter form $B$ is the symmetric bilinear form determined by $B(e_s,e_s)=1$, $B(e_s,e_t)=-\cos(\pi/m(s,t))$ for distinct $s,t$ with finite $m(s,t)$, and $B(e_s,e_t)=-1$ when $m(s,t)=\infty$. Put $r_s(v)=v-2B(v,e_s)e_s$. The canonical real reflection representation is the homomorphism $\rho:W\to\mathrm{GL}(V)$ satisfying $\rho(s)=r_s$. Here $\mathrm{GL}(V)$ is the group of invertible linear maps from $V$ to itself. Write $wv$ for $\rho(w)v$, $\alpha_s=e_s$, and call the elements of $\Phi=\{we_s:w\in W,\ s\in S\}$ roots.

Let $\Theta=V^*$ be the algebraic dual, the space of all real-valued linear functionals on $V$. The contragredient action is $(w f)(v)=f(\rho(w)^{-1}v)$ for $w\in W$, $f\in\Theta$, and $v\in V$. The closed chamber is $C=\{f\in\Theta:f(e_s)\geq0\text{ for all }s\in S\}$, and the open chamber is $C^\circ=\{f\in\Theta:f(e_s)>0\text{ for all }s\in S\}$. For $I\subseteq S$, its face of type $I$ is $C_I=\{f\in\Theta:f(e_s)=0\text{ for }s\in I,\ f(e_s)>0\text{ for }s\notin I\}$. For $\alpha\in\Phi$, the root hyperplane is $H_\alpha=\{f\in\Theta:f(\alpha)=0\}$.

No nondegeneracy of $B$ is assumed, and $V$ is not identified with $V^*$ using $B$. These conventions apply to finite $S$; no infinite-rank extension is asserted here.

Let $V=\mathbb R^S$, the space of real-valued functions on $S$, and let $e_s$ be the function that is $1$ at $s$ and $0$ elsewhere. The Coxeter form $B$ is the symmetric bilinear form determined by $B(e_s,e_s)=1$, $B(e_s,e_t)=-\cos(\pi/m(s,t))$ for distinct $s,t$ with finite $m(s,t)$, and $B(e_s,e_t)=-1$ when $m(s,t)=\infty$. Put $r_s(v)=v-2B(v,e_s)e_s$. The canonical real reflection representation is the homomorphism $\rho:W\to\mathrm{GL}(V)$ satisfying $\rho(s)=r_s$. Here $\mathrm{GL}(V)$ is the group of invertible linear maps from $V$ to itself. Write $wv$ for $\rho(w)v$, $\alpha_s=e_s$, and call the elements of $\Phi=\{we_s:w\in W,\ s\in S\}$ roots.

Let $\Theta=V^*$ be the algebraic dual, the space of all real-valued linear functionals on $V$. The contragredient action is $(w f)(v)=f(\rho(w)^{-1}v)$ for $w\in W$, $f\in\Theta$, and $v\in V$. The closed chamber is $C=\{f\in\Theta:f(e_s)\geq0\text{ for all }s\in S\}$, and the open chamber is $C^\circ=\{f\in\Theta:f(e_s)>0\text{ for all }s\in S\}$. For $I\subseteq S$, its face of type $I$ is $C_I=\{f\in\Theta:f(e_s)=0\text{ for }s\in I,\ f(e_s)>0\text{ for }s\notin I\}$. For $\alpha\in\Phi$, the root hyperplane is $H_\alpha=\{f\in\Theta:f(\alpha)=0\}$.

No nondegeneracy of $B$ is assumed, and $V$ is not identified with $V^*$ using $B$. These conventions apply to finite $S$; no infinite-rank extension is asserted here.

def-reduced-ribbon-artin-tits-normaliser.title: Reduced ribbon groupoid

statement.heading: Definition
statement.source_excerpt:
Let $\Gamma$ be a finite-rank spherical Coxeter diagram, meaning that its Coxeter group $W$ is finite, with vertex set $\Gamma_0$. Let $A$ be its Artin–Tits group and fix $J\subseteq\Gamma_0$. For $I\subseteq\Gamma_0$, write $W_I$ for the subgroup generated by the simple reflections indexed by $I$. An **associate** of $J$ is a subset $I$ for which $W_I$ is conjugate to $W_J$ in $W$.

Let $\mathcal R'(J)$ be the ribbon groupoid: its objects are the associates of $J$, and an arrow $I\to K$ is an element $\beta\in A$ with $A_I^+\beta=\beta A_K^+$, tagged with its source and target. Here $A_I^+$ is the submonoid generated by the standard Artin generators indexed by $I$. Composition is multiplication from left to right.

For an associate $I$ and $a\in\Gamma_0\setminus I$, put $T=I\cup\{a\}$. Let $w_T$ be the longest element of $W_T$, let $\iota_T:T\to T$ be the opposition permutation defined by $w_T\alpha_i=-\alpha_{\iota_T(i)}$ on the simple roots, and put $K=T\setminus\{\iota_T(a)\}$. If $\Delta_L$ denotes the positive reduced-word lift in $A$ of the longest element of $W_L$, the elementary ribbon is $\mu_{a,I}=\Delta_I^{-1}\Delta_T$, regarded as an arrow $I\to K$ of $\mathcal R'(J)$.

The **reduced ribbon groupoid** $\mathcal R(J)$ is the subgroupoid of $\mathcal R'(J)$ with all the same objects whose arrows are finite composable products of the arrows $\mu_{a,I}$ and their inverses, including empty products as identities. Equivalently, it is the smallest subgroupoid of $\mathcal R'(J)$ containing every object and every such elementary ribbon arrow.

def-relative-complement-artin-tits-norma.title: Relative complexified hyperplane complement

statement.heading: Definition
statement.source_excerpt:
Let $(W,S)$ be a Coxeter system with finite $S$, and let $J\subseteq S$. In the real dual representation space $\Theta$, let $\Theta_J$ be the subspace on which the simple roots indexed by $J$ vanish. Let $\mathrm{Cone}(J)$ be the intersection of the Tits cone with $\Theta_J$, and let $\mathrm{Cone}(J)^\circ$ be its interior in $\Theta_J$. Let $\mathcal H^J$ be the set of distinct hyperplanes obtained by restricting to $\Theta_J$ those root hyperplanes that do not contain $\Theta_J$.

The **relative complexified hyperplane complement** is the space

$$\mathcal X_J^{\mathbb C}=(\mathrm{Cone}(J)^\circ\times\mathrm{Cone}(J)^\circ)\setminus\bigcup_{H\in\mathcal H^J}(H\times H).$$

It has the subspace topology inherited from the product topology. If $W$ is finite, a case also called **spherical type**, then $\mathrm{Cone}(J)^\circ=\Theta_J$. Under the real-linear identification $(x,y)\mapsto x\otimes1+y\otimes i$ of $\Theta_J\times\Theta_J$ with $\Theta_J\otimes_{\mathbb R}\mathbb C$, the space is

$$(\Theta_J\otimes_{\mathbb R}\mathbb C)\setminus\bigcup_{H\in\mathcal H^J}(H\otimes_{\mathbb R}\mathbb C).$$
