def-relative-cone-artin-tits-normalisers.title: Tits cone intersections, relative roots and arrangements

statement.heading: Definition
statement.source_excerpt:
Let $\Gamma_0$ be finite, with Coxeter group $W$, real simple-root basis $(\alpha_i)_{i\in\Gamma_0}$, root set $\Phi=\Phi^+\sqcup\Phi^-$ and dual space $\Theta$. For $J\subseteq\Gamma_0$, let $\Theta_J=\{f\in\Theta:f(\alpha_j)=0\text{ for every }j\in J\}$ and let $\Phi_J=\{w\alpha_j:w\in W_J,\ j\in J\}$, where $W_J$ is the subgroup generated by the simple reflections indexed by $J$. Write $H_\alpha=\{f\in\Theta:f(\alpha)=0\}$ and $\mathcal H=\{H_\alpha:\alpha\in\Phi\}$, and let $\mathrm{Cone}$ be the Tits cone, the union of the $W$-translates of the closed fundamental chamber.

The **Tits cone intersection**, or **$J$-cone**, is $\mathrm{Cone}(J)=\mathrm{Cone}\cap\Theta_J$. Its relative interior $\mathrm{Cone}(J)^\circ$ is its interior in $\Theta_J$, equipped with the topology induced from the coordinate Euclidean topology on $\Theta$.

The **relative roots**, or **$J$-roots**, and their positive and negative parts are
$$\Phi^J=\{\alpha\in\Phi:\Theta_J\not\subseteq H_\alpha\}=\Phi\setminus\Phi_J,\qquad \Phi^J_\pm=\Phi^J\cap\Phi^\pm.$$
The **relative arrangement** is the set of distinct hyperplanes in $\Theta_J$
$$\mathcal H^J=\{H\cap\Theta_J:H\in\mathcal H,\ \Theta_J\not\subseteq H\}=\{H_\alpha\cap\Theta_J:\alpha\in\Phi^J_+\}.$$
Different positive relative roots may give the same restricted hyperplane. When $J=\varnothing$, the pair $(\mathrm{Cone}(J)^\circ,\mathcal H^J)$ is $(\mathrm{Cone}^\circ,\mathcal H)$, the Coxeter arrangement in the interior of the Tits cone.

Relative roots are those whose hyperplanes do not contain the subspace; the relative arrangement consists of the corresponding restricted hyperplanes. The empty-subset case recovers the Coxeter arrangement.

statement.heading: Definition
statement.source_excerpt:
Let $\Gamma$ be a spherical Coxeter diagram, meaning that its Coxeter group $W$ is finite, with vertex set $\Gamma_0$ and associated Artin–Tits group $A$. Let $A^+$ be the submonoid of $A$ generated by the standard Artin generators. For $J\subseteq\Gamma_0$, let $w_J$ be the longest element of the standard parabolic subgroup $W_J$, and let $\Delta_J$ be its positive reduced-word lift in $A$.

Let $I\subseteq\Gamma_0$ and $a\in I^c=\Gamma_0\setminus I$. Write $I+a=I\cup\{a\}$, and let $[I,a]$ be the vertex set of the connected component containing $a$ in the diagram induced on $I+a$. Write $[I,a]-a=[I,a]\setminus\{a\}$. The **positive elementary ribbon element** associated to $(a,I)$ is

$$\mu_{a,I}=\Delta_{[I,a]-a}^{-1}\Delta_{[I,a]}\in A^+.$$

Equivalently, $\mu_{a,I}=\Delta_I^{-1}\Delta_{I+a}$. Inverses and products in these expressions are taken in $A$.

statement.heading: Definition
statement.source_excerpt:
Let $\Gamma$ be a finite-rank spherical Coxeter diagram, meaning that its Coxeter group $W$ is finite, with vertex set $\Gamma_0$. Let $A$ be its Artin–Tits group, with generators $\sigma_i$ indexed by $i\in\Gamma_0$, and let $A_I^+$ be the submonoid generated by the $\sigma_i$ for $i\in I$. Fix $J\subseteq\Gamma_0$. An associate of $J$ is a subset $I\subseteq\Gamma_0$ whose standard Coxeter parabolic subgroup $W_I=\langle s_i:i\in I\rangle$ is conjugate to $W_J$ in $W$.

The **ribbon groupoid** $\mathcal R'(J)$ has the associates of $J$ as objects. For associates $I,K$, its arrows $I\to K$ are tagged by source and target and have labels

def-separating-hyperplane-artin-tits-nor.title: Separation by a hyperplane

statement.heading: Definition
statement.source_excerpt:
Use the finite-rank Coxeter realization, dual space $\Theta$ with its Euclidean topology, and full Tits cone $\mathrm{Cone}\subseteq\Theta$ of [def-coxeter-arrangement-artin-tits-normalisers](item-def-coxeter-arrangement-artin-tits-normalisers). Let $H\subseteq\Theta$ be a linear hyperplane, and choose a nonzero linear functional $a:\Theta\to\mathbb R$ with $H=\ker a$. Its two open half-spaces are $\{x\in\Theta:a(x)>0\}$ and $\{x\in\Theta:a(x)<0\}$.

For $f,g\in\mathrm{Cone}$, say that $H$ separates $f$ and $g$ if $a(f)$ and $a(g)$ have opposite strict signs. Equivalently, $f$ and $g$ belong to different connected components of $\mathrm{Cone}\setminus H$, equipped with the subspace topology. In particular, a point of $H$ is not separated from any point by $H$.

def-set-notation-artin-tits-normalisers.title: Subset and vertex-complement notation

statement.heading: Definition
statement.source_excerpt:
Let $X$ and $a$ be sets. The singleton $\{a\}$ is the set whose only element is $a$. Write $X+a=X\cup\{a\}$ and $X-a=X\setminus\{a\}$. Thus $X+a$ consists of the elements of $X$ together with $a$, while $X-a$ consists of the elements of $X$ other than $a$; no assumption that $a\in X$ is required.

Let $\Gamma_0$ be the vertex set of the Coxeter diagram $\Gamma$. For $I\subseteq\Gamma_0$, write $I^c=\Gamma_0\setminus I$ for the complement of $I$ relative to $\Gamma_0$, namely the set of vertices of $\Gamma$ that are not in $I$.

def-simple-wall-crossing-artin-tits-norm.title: Simple wall-crossing elements and maps

statement.heading: Definition
statement.source_excerpt:
Let $(W,S)$ be a Coxeter system indexed by the vertex set $\Gamma_0$, and fix $J\subseteq\Gamma_0$. Write $W_L$ for the subgroup generated by the simple generators indexed by $L\subseteq\Gamma_0$. Let $(x,I)\in\mathrm{Cham}(J)$, where $\mathrm{Cham}(J)$ is the algebraic chamber-label set: $W_Jx=xW_I$ and $x$ has minimum length in $xW_I$.

Choose $a\in\Gamma_0\setminus I$. Put $D=[I,a]$, the vertices of the connected component containing $a$ in the Coxeter diagram induced on $I\cup\{a\}$, and suppose $W_D$ is finite. For each finite standard parabolic $W_L$, write $w_L$ for its longest element and $\iota_L$ for the permutation of $L$ determined by $w_L\alpha_i=-\alpha_{\iota_L(i)}$ on its simple roots. Define the **simple wall-crossing element** and its associated pair by

$$v_{a,I}=w_{D\setminus\{a\}}w_D,\qquad K=(I\cup\{a\})\setminus\{\iota_D(a)\},\qquad \omega_{a,I}(x,I)=(xv_{a,I},K).$$

For fixed $J$, $I$ and $a$, this defines $\omega_{a,I}$ on the labels $(x,I)\in\mathrm{Cham}(J)$ satisfying the stated finiteness condition, with values in $W\times\mathcal P(\Gamma_0)$, where $\mathcal P(\Gamma_0)$ denotes the set of all subsets of $\Gamma_0$.

def-small-groupoid-interface-artin-tits-.title: Set-sized groupoids, functors and composition conversion

statement.heading: Definition
statement.source_excerpt:
A small category is a category whose objects and morphisms each form a set; each morphism carries its source and target. A groupoid is a category in which every morphism has a two-sided inverse. A groupoid is connected when it is nonempty and there is an arrow between every ordered pair of objects.

For arrows $a:x\to y$ and $b:y\to z$, write $ab=b\circ a$; hence composition is read from left to right. A covariant functor sends objects to objects and arrows to arrows with the corresponding sources and targets, preserving identities and composition. An automorphism is a functor from a category to itself with a two-sided inverse functor.

For an object $x$ of a small groupoid $\mathcal G$, its vertex group $\mathcal G_x$ is the set of arrows $x\to x$ with the left-to-right product and identity $1_x$. Given an arrow $a:x\to y$, the associated conjugation map $c_a:\mathcal G_x\to\mathcal G_y$ is $c_a(u)=a^{-1}ua$.

def-standard-expressions-artin-tits-norm.title: Standard expressions and their lengths

statement.heading: Definition
statement.source_excerpt:
Let $(W,S)$ be a Coxeter system with diagram vertex set $\Gamma_0$, and fix $J\subseteq\Gamma_0$. For $L\subseteq\Gamma_0$, write $W_L=\langle s_i:i\in L\rangle$; an associate of $J$ is a subset whose standard parabolic subgroup is conjugate to $W_J$. The Brink–Howlett groupoid $\mathcal{BH}(J)$ has these associates as objects. A morphism $x:I\to K$ is labelled by an element $x\in W$ satisfying $\{x\alpha_k:k\in K\}=\{\alpha_i:i\in I\}$, and composable labels multiply from left to right. Write $\ell(x)$ for the least number of simple generators in a word representing $x$.

For an associate $I$ and $a\in\Gamma_0\setminus I$, let $D=[I,a]$ be the component containing $a$ in the diagram induced on $I\cup\{a\}$. If $W_D$ is finite, write $w_L$ for the longest element of a finite $W_L$ and $\iota_D$ for the permutation defined by $w_D\alpha_i=-\alpha_{\iota_D(i)}$. Put $v_{a,I}=w_{D\setminus\{a\}}w_D$ and $I'=(I\cup\{a\})\setminus\{\iota_D(a)\}$. This label is a morphism $I\to I'$.

For objects $I,K$ and a morphism $w:I\to K$, a **standard expression** is a finite sequence of such morphisms $v_{a_1,I_1},\ldots,v_{a_m,I_m}$, composable in that order from $I$ to $K$, whose product is $w$ and for which $\ell(w)=\sum_{i=1}^m\ell(v_{a_i,I_i})$. For $m>0$ the source condition says $I_1=I$. The empty sequence is allowed when $I=K$ and $w$ is the identity; its product is the identity and its length sum is zero. The **standard-expression length of the expression** is its number $m$ of factors. When a morphism has a standard expression and every standard expression for it has the same number of factors, this common number is denoted $\ell_{\mathcal{BH}}(w)$ and called the standard-expression length of $w$.

def-topological-path-assignment-artin-ti.title: Equivariant chamber-point and path assignment

statement.heading: Definition
statement.source_excerpt:
Let $(W,S)$ be a Coxeter system with finite $W$, let $J\subseteq S$, and put $G=N(W,J)=\operatorname{Norm}_W(W_J)/W_J$, where $W_J$ is generated by $J$. Use the relative real space $E$, its finite hyperplane arrangement $\mathcal H^J$, and its complexified complement $\mathcal X_J^{\mathbb C}$ from [def-relative-complement-artin-tits-normalisers](item-def-relative-complement-artin-tits-normalisers). A chamber is a connected component of $E\setminus\bigcup_{H\in\mathcal H^J}H$; two chambers are adjacent if they share a wall. For each chamber $C$ use its open set $X_C$, and for an ordered adjacent pair $(C,C')$ use the specified component $X_{C,C'}\subseteq X_C\cap X_{C'}$, as defined in [def-chamber-open-sets-artin-tits-normalisers](item-def-chamber-open-sets-artin-tits-normalisers).

Choose points $a_C\in X_C$ satisfying $a_{gC}=g a_C$ for every $g\in G$. Assign $C$ to $a_C$. For a directed arrow $C\to C'$ between adjacent chambers, choose $d\in X_{C,C'}$, a continuous path $\gamma_1:[0,1]\to X_C$ from $a_C$ to $d$, and a continuous path $\gamma_2:[0,1]\to X_{C'}$ from $d$ to $a_{C'}$. Assign the arrow the endpoint-fixed homotopy class $[\gamma_1\gamma_2]$ of their concatenation in $\mathcal X_J^{\mathbb C}$, traversing $\gamma_1$ first. An endpoint-fixed homotopy is a continuous deformation through paths with the same two endpoints; these classes are the arrows of the fundamental groupoid $\pi_1(\mathcal X_J^{\mathbb C})$.

The assignment on directed arrows is independent of the choices of $d,\gamma_1,\gamma_2$ once the $a_C$ are fixed, and it is $G$-equivariant. It is an assignment on the directed chamber graph; no claim that it respects the positive category's relations or gives an equivalence is made in this definition.

statement.heading: Definition
statement.source_excerpt:
Let $(W,S)$ be a Coxeter system with finite $W$, let $J\subseteq S$, and put $G=N(W,J)=\operatorname{Norm}_W(W_J)/W_J$, where $W_J$ is generated by $J$. Use the relative real space $E$, its finite hyperplane arrangement $\mathcal H^J$, and its complexified complement $\mathcal X_J^{\mathbb C}$ from [[def-relative-complement-artin-tits-normalisers]]. A chamber is a connected component of $E\setminus\bigcup_{H\in\mathcal H^J}H$; two chambers are adjacent if they share a wall. For each chamber $C$ use its open set $X_C$, and for an ordered adjacent pair $(C,C')$ use the specified component $X_{C,C'}\subseteq X_C\cap X_{C'}$, as defined in [[def-chamber-open-sets-artin-tits-normalisers]].

Choose points $a_C\in X_C$ satisfying $a_{gC}=g a_C$ for every $g\in G$. Assign $C$ to $a_C$. For a directed arrow $C\to C'$ between adjacent chambers, choose $d\in X_{C,C'}$, a continuous path $\gamma_1:[0,1]\to X_C$ from $a_C$ to $d$, and a continuous path $\gamma_2:[0,1]\to X_{C'}$ from $d$ to $a_{C'}$. Assign the arrow the endpoint-fixed homotopy class $[\gamma_1\gamma_2]$ of their concatenation in $\mathcal X_J^{\mathbb C}$, traversing $\gamma_1$ first. An endpoint-fixed homotopy is a continuous deformation through paths with the same two endpoints; these classes are the arrows of the fundamental groupoid $\pi_1(\mathcal X_J^{\mathbb C})$.

The assignment on directed arrows is independent of the choices of $d,\gamma_1,\gamma_2$ once the $a_C$ are fixed, and it is $G$-equivariant. It is an assignment on the directed chamber graph; no claim that it respects the positive category's relations or gives an equivalence is made in this definition.

def-universal-wall-groupoid-artin-tits-n.title: Universal wall groupoid on relative chambers

statement.heading: Definition
statement.source_excerpt:
Let $(W,S)$ be a Coxeter system, let $J$ be a subset of its diagram's vertex set, and let $\mathrm{Cham}(J)$ be the algebraic chamber-label set. Thus its elements are pairs $(x,I)$ with $x\in W$, $W_Jx=xW_I$, and $x$ of minimal length in $xW_I$.

The **universal wall groupoid** $\widetilde{\mathcal{BH}}(J)$ has object set $\mathrm{Cham}(J)$. For objects $A=(x,I)$ and $B=(y,K)$, its hom-set $\operatorname{Hom}(A,B)$ is the singleton whose arrow is labelled $x^{-1}y\in W$. Arrows are tagged by their source and target, even when their labels in $W$ coincide. Composition is read from left to right: the arrow $A\to B$ labelled $x^{-1}y$ followed by the arrow $B\to C=(z,L)$ labelled $y^{-1}z$ is the arrow $A\to C$ labelled $(x^{-1}y)(y^{-1}z)=x^{-1}z$.

For the geometric interpretation, assume additionally that $(W,S)$ has finite rank. Identify the labels with the relative chambers by the chamber-labelling bijection, and call two labels adjacent when their corresponding chambers share a wall. For adjacent labels $A=(x,I)$ and $B=(y,K)$, let $a\notin I$ be the wall index supplied by the adjacent-wall proposition. That proposition supplies finiteness of the standard parabolic on the crossing component, as required to define the simple wall-crossing element $v_{a,I}$. The unique arrow $A\to B$ has label $v_{a,I}$. No finiteness of $W$, $W_I$ or $W_{I\cup\{a\}}$ is assumed.

ex-a3-arrangement-artin-tits-normalisers.title: A3 relative arrangement and its six labelled chambers

statement.heading: Example
statement.source_excerpt:
Take the type $A_3$ Coxeter system with vertices $1,2,3$ in a chain, simple reflections $s_1,s_2,s_3$, simple roots $\alpha_1,\alpha_2,\alpha_3$, and dual basis $\alpha_1^*,\alpha_2^*,\alpha_3^*$. Let $J=\{3\}$. Then $\Theta_J=\mathbb R\alpha_1^*\oplus\mathbb R\alpha_2^*=\mathrm{Cone}(J)=\mathrm{Cone}(J)^\circ$. Its relative arrangement consists of the three lines $\mathbb R\alpha_2^*$, $\mathbb R\alpha_1^*$ and $\mathbb R(\alpha_1^*-\alpha_2^*)$, obtained respectively from $\alpha_1$, $\alpha_2$ and $\alpha_1+\alpha_2$.

The six chambers are the connected components of the complement of these lines. Counterclockwise from the positive quadrant, their labels are $(e,3)$, $(s_1,3)$, $(s_1s_2s_3,2)$, $(s_1s_2s_3s_1s_2,1)$, $(s_2s_3s_1s_2,1)$ and $(s_2s_3,2)$. Here $e$ is the identity and a numeral in the second position abbreviates the corresponding singleton subset.

ex-a3-doubled-graph-artin-tits-normalise.title: A3 doubled adjacency graph

statement.heading: Example
statement.source_excerpt:
Take the type $A_3$ Coxeter system with vertices $1,2,3$ in a chain and $J=\{3\}$. Write a numeral in a chamber label for the corresponding singleton subset. In cyclic order, put $C_0=(e,3)$, $C_1=(s_1,3)$, $C_2=(s_1s_2s_3,2)$, $C_3=(s_1s_2s_3s_1s_2,1)$, $C_4=(s_2s_3s_1s_2,1)$ and $C_5=(s_2s_3,2)$. The directed chamber graph is a doubled hexagon: for each $i$ modulo $6$ it has one arrow $C_i\to C_{i+1}$ and one arrow $C_{i+1}\to C_i$, and no other arrows.

The labels of the forward arrows, in the order $i=0,\ldots,5$, are $\omega_{1,3},\omega_{2,3},\omega_{1,2},\omega_{3,1},\omega_{2,1},\omega_{3,2}$. The corresponding reverse-arrow labels are $\omega_{1,3},\omega_{3,2},\omega_{2,1},\omega_{3,1},\omega_{1,2},\omega_{2,3}$. Here $\omega_{a,I}$ denotes the simple wall crossing from a label with second component $I$ at the index $a\notin I$; the numeral in its second subscript abbreviates the singleton $I$.

ex-d4-atomic-relations-artin-tits-normal.title: Explicit D4 atomic braid relations and lifted paths

statement.heading: Example
statement.source_excerpt:
Use $D_4$ with central generator $t=s_2$, leaves $s=s_1,u=s_3,v=s_4$, and $J=\{2\}$. Write $(x,i)$ for a chamber label and compose arrow labels in traversal order. The two atomic braid relations associated with the displayed hexagon are

$$st\cdot v\cdot ts=vt\cdot s\cdot tv,\qquad s\cdot tv\cdot st=tv\cdot st\cdot v.$$

The first lifts to

$$(e,2)\to(st,1)\to(stv,1)\to(stvts,2),$$

$$(e,2)\to(vt,4)\to(vts,4)\to(stvts,2).$$

The second lifts to

$$(vts,4)\to(vt,4)\to(e,2)\to(st,1),$$

$$(vts,4)\to(stvts,2)\to(stv,1)\to(st,1).$$

These are the two opposite length-three arcs from each specified starting vertex around the same hexagonal face. Every atomic braid relation in this example has two or three factors on each side, corresponding respectively to square or hexagonal faces around codimension-two flats. Here a codimension-two flat is a one-dimensional intersection of supporting hyperplanes in the three-dimensional relative space; a normal two-dimensional slice at a nonzero generic point of the flat sees the polygonal chamber cycle.

ex-d4-cell-complex-artin-tits-normaliser.title: The D4 groupoid and the spherical cell complex

statement.heading: Statement
statement.source_excerpt:
For the $D_4$ example with central $J=\{2\}$, fill every polygonal face of the undirected chamber adjacency graph, including the outermost hexagon in its planar drawing. The resulting space $D$ is homeomorphic to $S^2$. Equivalently, retain two distinct directed edges per adjacency, attach one disk along each inverse two-cycle, and attach one polygon disk per cyclic face, using coherent boundary orientations as below. This doubled complex $K$ is also homeomorphic to $S^2$. The universal wall groupoid is isomorphic, on its 32 chamber objects, to $\Pi_1(K;V)$ and to $\Pi_1(D;V)$.

Here $V$ is the set of chamber vertices, and $\Pi_1(-;V)$ means the full subgroupoid of the fundamental groupoid whose objects are precisely $V$. A geometric face is filled once, regardless of the choice of a starting vertex or orientation of its boundary word. This makes the attachment convention explicit.

ex-d4-comparison-functors-artin-tits-nor.title: Explicit D4 comparison functors

statement.heading: Example
statement.source_excerpt:
Take the $D_4$ Coxeter system whose central vertex is $2$ and whose leaves are $1,3,4$, and put $J=\{2\}$. Let $W$ be its Coxeter group and $A$ its Artin–Tits group. The canonical homomorphism $\pi:A\to W$ sends each standard Artin generator to the corresponding simple reflection.

Let $\mathcal D$ be the Deligne groupoid of the relative chamber arrangement: its objects are the relative chambers, and it is the groupoid completion of the directed chamber-path category modulo identifications of geodesic paths with the same endpoints. A geodesic is a path of minimum length among paths with those endpoints. A chamber label $(x,I)$ consists of $x\in W$ and a subset $I$ with $W_Jx=xW_I$, where $W_I$ is generated by the simple reflections indexed by $I$ and $x$ has minimum length in $xW_I$. The universal wall groupoid $\widetilde{\mathcal{BH}}$ has these labels as objects and exactly one arrow from $(x,I)$ to $(y,K)$, labelled $x^{-1}y$.

Let $\mathcal R$ be the reduced ribbon groupoid. Its objects are the associates of $J$, meaning subsets $I$ for which $W_I$ is conjugate to $W_J$; its arrows are endpoint-tagged Artin-group elements generated by elementary ribbons and their inverses. The Brink–Howlett groupoid $\mathcal{BH}$ has the same objects, with an arrow $I\to K$ labelled by an element of $W$ carrying the simple-root set indexed by $K$ onto that indexed by $I$. In this example the objects of $\mathcal R$ are $\{1\},\{2\},\{3\},\{4\}$.

There is a functor $H:\mathcal D\to\widetilde{\mathcal{BH}}$ that is the identity on objects. For a directed chamber path $p:(x,I)\to(y,K)$, it sends the represented arrow to the unique arrow labelled $x^{-1}y=v_p$, where $v_p$ is the ordered product of the simple wall-crossing elements along $p$. On formal inverses, $H$ takes the inverse arrow. There is also a functor $P:\mathcal R\to\mathcal{BH}$, identity on objects, induced on arrow labels by $\pi:A\to W$.

Let $\mathcal D$ be the Deligne groupoid of the relative chamber arrangement: its objects are the relative chambers, and it is the groupoid completion of the directed chamber-path category modulo identifications of geodesic paths with the same endpoints. A geodesic is a path of minimum length among paths with those endpoints. A chamber label $(x,I)$ consists of $x\in W$ and a subset $I$ with $W_Jx=xW_I$, where $W_I$ is generated by the simple reflections indexed by $I$ and $x$ has minimum length in $xW_I$. The universal wall groupoid $\widetilde{\mathcal{BH}}$ has these labels as objects and exactly one arrow from $(x,I)$ to $(y,K)$, labelled $x^{-1}y$.

Let $\mathcal R$ be the reduced ribbon groupoid. Its objects are the associates of $J$, meaning subsets $I$ for which $W_I$ is conjugate to $W_J$; its arrows are endpoint-tagged Artin-group elements generated by elementary ribbons and their inverses. The Brink–Howlett groupoid $\mathcal{BH}$ has the same objects, with an arrow $I\to K$ labelled by an element of $W$ carrying the simple-root set indexed by $K$ onto that indexed by $I$. In this example the objects of $\mathcal R$ are $\{1\},\{2\},\{3\},\{4\}$.

There is a functor $H:\mathcal D\to\widetilde{\mathcal{BH}}$ that is the identity on objects. For a directed chamber path $p:(x,I)\to(y,K)$, it sends the represented arrow to the unique arrow labelled $x^{-1}y=v_p$, where $v_p$ is the ordered product of the simple wall-crossing elements along $p$. On formal inverses, $H$ takes the inverse arrow. There is also a functor $P:\mathcal R\to\mathcal{BH}$, identity on objects, induced on arrow labels by $\pi:A\to W$.

ex-d4-deligne-ribbon-presentations-artin.title: D4 Deligne and ribbon graphs without quadratic relations

statement.heading: Example
statement.source_excerpt:
Take the $D_4$ Coxeter system with central vertex $2$, leaves $1,3,4$, and $J=\{2\}$. Write $s=s_1$, $t=s_2$, $u=s_3$ and $v=s_4$. A chamber label $(x,i)$ means $(x,\{i\})$. Let $\mathcal D^+$ be the category of directed chamber paths modulo identifications of geodesics with common endpoints, and let $\mathcal D$ be its groupoid completion. A geodesic is a path of minimum length among paths with those endpoints. The reduced ribbon groupoid $\mathcal R$ has the associates of $J$ as objects and is generated by elementary ribbon arrows and their inverses.

The generating graph for $\mathcal D$ is the 32-vertex chamber adjacency graph of the preceding labelled-chamber example, with each edge replaced by one arrow in each direction. Its relations are generated by identifying the two geodesic arcs around each codimension-two face: these faces are squares or hexagons. In particular, both pairs of paths displayed in (7.2), with the second atomic relation corrected to $s\cdot tv\cdot st=tv\cdot st\cdot v$, commute in $\mathcal D^+$ and in $\mathcal D$.

The generating graph for $\mathcal R$ has objects $1,2,3,4$. Its nonloop arrows have Coxeter-word labels $st:2\to1$, $ts:1\to2$, $vt:2\to4$, $tv:4\to2$, $ut:2\to3$ and $tu:3\to2$; its loops are $u,v$ at $1$, $s,u$ at $4$, and $s,v$ at $3$. Each word denotes its positive Artin lift, obtained by replacing each letter by its Artin generator. The defining relations are the images of the square and hexagon relations. With $N(W,J)=\operatorname{Norm}_W(W_J)/W_J$, there is an isomorphism $\mathcal D/N(W,J)\cong\mathcal R$; the quotient functor $\mathcal D\to\mathcal R$ is a normal covering with deck group $N(W,J)$.

The two opposite generating arrows of a chamber edge are not mutual inverses in $\mathcal D$: their composite is nonidentity. Likewise, every positive two-cycle in the displayed ribbon graph, including going twice around a loop, is nonidentity in $\mathcal R$. In particular $s^2=e$ in $W$, while $\sigma_s^2\ne e$ in the Artin group.

ex-d4-normaliser-orbits-artin-tits-norma.title: Four colour orbits of eight D4 chambers

statement.heading: Example
statement.source_excerpt:
Take the $D_4$ Coxeter diagram with central vertex $2$ and $J=\{2\}$. Let $W_I$ denote the subgroup generated by the simple reflections indexed by $I$, and put $N(W,J)=\operatorname{Norm}_W(W_J)/W_J$. The relative chambers are labelled by pairs $(x,I)$ with $W_Jx=xW_I$ and $x$ the minimum-length element of $xW_I$; write $(x,i)$ for $(x,\{i\})$.

The action of $N(W,J)$ on these chambers has four orbits, each containing eight chambers. Their second labels are respectively $\{1\},\{2\},\{3\},\{4\}$: these are precisely the associates of $J$, meaning the objects of the Brink–Howlett groupoid. In Figures 2–3 of the article, equal colours denote equal second labels: black denotes $1$, red $2$, green $3$ and blue $4$.

The universal Brink–Howlett covering sends the object $(x,I)$ to $I$ and the arrow from $(x,I)$ to $(y,K)$ labelled $x^{-1}y$ to the arrow with the same label $x^{-1}y$ from $I$ to $K$.

ex-d4-normaliser-vertex-group-artin-tits.title: Eight-element D4 normaliser quotient vertex group

statement.heading: Example
statement.source_excerpt:
For any finite-rank Coxeter system in the conventions of [prop-chambers-morphisms-artin-tits-normalisers](item-prop-chambers-morphisms-artin-tits-normalisers), an arrow $x:J\to I$ of the Brink–Howlett groupoid $\mathcal{BH}(J)$ lifts uniquely from the fundamental label $(e,J)$ to the label $(x,I)$.

For the $D_4$ Coxeter diagram with central vertex $2$, set $J=\{2\}$ and write $s=s_1$, $t=s_2$, $u=s_3$, $v=s_4$, and $e=1$. Abbreviate $(x,\{2\})$ to $(x,2)$. Let $W_J=\langle t\rangle$, let $\operatorname{Norm}_W(W_J)=\{w\in W:wW_Jw^{-1}=W_J\}$, and put $N(W,J)=\operatorname{Norm}_W(W_J)/W_J$. Then the vertex group $\mathcal{BH}_J=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{BH}(J)}(J,J)$ is a subgroup of $W$, and the quotient map induces $\mathcal{BH}_J\cong N(W,J)$. More precisely,

$$\mathcal{BH}_J=\{x:(x,2)\in\mathrm{Cham}(J)\}=\{e,stuts,stuvts,stvts,vtsutv,stuvtsutvtu,vtutv,utsvtu\}.$$

These are eight distinct group elements. The eight corresponding labels are the red vertices in the article's figure.

ex-d4-positive-roots-artin-tits-normalis.title: The twelve D4 positive roots

statement.heading: Example
statement.source_excerpt: Let $W$ be the Coxeter group with the $D_4$ diagram whose central vertex $2$ is joined to $1,3,4$. In its standard real reflection representation let $\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_4$ be the simple-root basis, and let $\Phi=\{w\alpha_i:w\in W,\ 1\leq i\leq4\}$. A positive root is a root whose coordinates in this basis are all nonnegative. Then $\Phi^+=\{\alpha_1,\alpha_2,\alpha_3,\alpha_4,\alpha_1+\alpha_2,\alpha_3+\alpha_2,\alpha_4+\alpha_2,\alpha_1+\alpha_2+\alpha_3,\alpha_1+\alpha_2+\alpha_4,\alpha_3+\alpha_2+\alpha_4,\alpha_1+\alpha_2+\alpha_3+\alpha_4,\alpha_1+2\alpha_2+\alpha_3+\alpha_4\}$.

ex-d4-quotient-graph-artin-tits-normalis.title: D4 Brink–Howlett generating graph

statement.heading: Example
statement.source_excerpt:
Use the $D_4$ Coxeter system with central vertex $2$, $J=\{2\}$, and simple reflections $s=s_1$, $t=s_2$, $u=s_3$, $v=s_4$. The Brink–Howlett groupoid is the quotient of the universal chamber groupoid by the normaliser quotient $N(W,J)=\operatorname{Norm}_W(W_J)/W_J$. Its generating graph has the four objects $1,2,3,4$, where $i$ denotes the singleton $\{i\}$.

Identifying the same-coloured vertices of the universal chamber graph gives this four-object graph. Its nonloop generators are $st:2\to1$, $ts:1\to2$, $vt:2\to4$, $tv:4\to2$, $ut:2\to3$ and $tu:3\to2$. Its loops are $u,v$ at object $1$, $s,u$ at object $4$, and $s,v$ at object $3$. Opposite arrows are labelled by inverse elements.

ex-d4-restricted-arrangement-artin-tits-.title: Seven relative D4 hyperplanes and thirty-two chambers

statement.heading: Example
statement.source_excerpt:
Use the $D_4$ data with central vertex $2$ and $J=\{2\}$. Then $\mathrm{Cone}(J)^\circ=\mathrm{Cone}(J)=\Theta_J=H_{\alpha_2}$ and the positive $J$-roots are $\Phi^+\setminus\{\alpha_2\}$. Different roots can restrict to the same hyperplane; for example, $H_{\alpha_1}\cap H_{\alpha_2}=H_{\alpha_1+\alpha_2}\cap H_{\alpha_2}$. The seven distinct relative hyperplanes are represented by $\alpha_1,\alpha_3,\alpha_4,\alpha_1+\alpha_2+\alpha_3,\alpha_1+\alpha_2+\alpha_4,\alpha_2+\alpha_3+\alpha_4,\alpha_1+\alpha_2+\alpha_3+\alpha_4$. Their complement in $\Theta_J$ has $32$ chambers, meaning connected components.

For $f\in\Theta_J$, the values $x=f(\alpha_1)$, $y=f(\alpha_3)$ and $z=f(\alpha_4)$ are independent coordinates, and the seven relative hyperplanes are the kernels of $x,y,z,x+y,x+z,y+z,x+y+z$. The chambers are precisely the nonempty strict sign regions of these seven forms: for signs $\epsilon_\ell\in\{1,-1\}$, the corresponding region consists of the points satisfying $\epsilon_\ell\ell>0$ for every one of the seven forms $\ell$.

ex-d4-universal-wall-graph-artin-tits-no.title: Universal groupoid interpretation of the D4 graph

statement.heading: Example
statement.source_excerpt:
Use the $D_4$ Coxeter system with central vertex $2$, $J=\{2\}$, and generators $s=s_1$, $t=s_2$, $u=s_3$, $v=s_4$ from [def-d4-example-data-artin-tits-normalisers](item-def-d4-example-data-artin-tits-normalisers). Take the 32 labelled vertices and 48 undirected adjacency pairs of [ex-d4-labelled-chamber-graph-artin-tits-normalisers](item-ex-d4-labelled-chamber-graph-artin-tits-normalisers), replacing each adjacency by an arrow in each direction. A path is a finite composable sequence of these arrows, including the empty path at a vertex.

The universal wall groupoid $\widetilde{\mathcal{BH}}(J)$ has exactly one morphism between each ordered pair of these vertices. It is presented by this directed graph with a relation identifying every two paths with the same endpoints. For an arrow from $A=(x,I)$ to an adjacent vertex $B=(y,K)$, its label in $W$ is $x^{-1}y=v_{a,I}$, where $a$ is the wall index at $A$; the reverse arrow has label $y^{-1}x=v_{b,K}$ for its wall index $b$ at $B$. Every two-cycle is an identity, and the two labels are inverses, although they need not be equal.

ex-nonlocal-finiteness-artin-tits-normal.title: Failure of local finiteness on the full cone

statement.heading: Statement
statement.source_excerpt:
Let $(W,S)$ be a Coxeter system with $S$ finite, in its canonical real Coxeter representation. Let $\Phi_+$ be its positive roots, $H_\alpha=\{f\in V^*:f(\alpha)=0\}$, and $\mathrm{Cone}$ the union of the translates of the closed fundamental chamber. For $J=\varnothing$, the relative cone is $\mathrm{Cone}$ and the relative hyperplanes are the distinct root hyperplanes $\mathcal H=\{H_\alpha:\alpha\in\Phi_+\}$. If $W$ is infinite, $\mathcal H$ is infinite and the arrangement $(\mathrm{Cone},\mathcal H)$ is not locally finite at the origin.

Here local finiteness at a point means that some neighborhood of the point in the subspace topology on $\mathrm{Cone}$ meets only finitely many distinct members of $\mathcal H$.

lem-author-1c4d8f320a61-minimum-normalis.title: Minimum representatives of normaliser cosets preserve the simple roots

statement.heading: Statement
statement.source_excerpt:
Let $(W,S)$ be an arbitrary-rank Coxeter system in its standard real root representation, with simple roots $\Pi=\{\alpha_i:i\in\Gamma_0\}$ and length $\ell$. Fix $J\subseteq\Gamma_0$, put $A_J=\{\alpha_j:j\in J\}$ and $W_J=\langle s_j:j\in J\rangle$, and write $M=\operatorname{Norm}_W(W_J)$ and $N_J=\{n\in W:nA_J=A_J\}$. These are the conventions of [def-normaliser-complement-artin-tits-normalisers](item-def-normaliser-complement-artin-tits-normalisers); $N_J$ is a subgroup of $M$.

For every $g\in M$, the coset $gW_J$ has a unique minimum-length element $d$, and $dA_J=A_J$. In particular $d\in N_J$.

source_references.title: Matthew Dyer and Harrison Gimenez, Root systems, Tits cones and imaginary cones of Brink–Howlett groupoids
source_references.locator: §1.4, PDF p.4; Proposition 2.10(b),(d) and Proposition 2.11(c), PDF p.23
source_references.statement: Dyer–Gimenez, Proposition 2.10(b),(d), states that for a reflection subgroup $U$ and $x\in W$, the coset $xU$ has a unique minimum-length element $d$ and the canonical simple system satisfies $\Pi_{xUx^{-1}}=d\Pi_U$. Proposition 2.11(c) states that for the standard parabolic subgroup $W_J$, its canonical simple system is $\Pi_{W_J}=A_J$. Here the canonical simple system is the distinguished positive simple-root system of the reflection subgroup in the ambient based root system.
source_references.hypotheses: Arbitrary-rank Coxeter system with standard based root system; arbitrary subset of simple roots; W_J is a reflection subgroup. No sphericity or finite-rank assumption.

Only the exact stated inputs and their application are checked; the older works cited there were not read, and no reconstruction of their proofs or visual PDF inspection is claimed. Infinite rank is explicitly permitted in §1.4.

Let $(W,S)$ be an arbitrary-rank Coxeter system in its standard real root representation, with simple roots $\Pi=\{\alpha_i:i\in\Gamma_0\}$ and length $\ell$. Fix $J\subseteq\Gamma_0$, put $A_J=\{\alpha_j:j\in J\}$ and $W_J=\langle s_j:j\in J\rangle$, and write $M=\operatorname{Norm}_W(W_J)$ and $N_J=\{n\in W:nA_J=A_J\}$. These are the conventions of [[def-normaliser-complement-artin-tits-normalisers]]; $N_J$ is a subgroup of $M$.

Each coset $gW_J$ with $g\in M$ contains exactly one element of $N_J$.

lem-author-2e40db4c81b4-lift-fibres.title: Unique lifts, endpoint fibres and characteristic subgroups

statement.heading: Statement
statement.source_excerpt: Let $p:E\to G$ be a functor of small groupoids, with $E,G$ connected and nonempty, bijective from the arrows with source $e$ to those with source $p(e)$ for every $e$. Such a functor is called a covering. Put $x=p(e)$ and $H=p(E_e)\le G_x$ (the characteristic subgroup at $e$). Products of arrows are read left to right. Lifts preserve products and inverses, $E_e\to G_x$ is injective, and two arrows $a,b:x\to y$ lifted from $e$ have equal endpoints exactly when $ab^{-1}\in H$.

lem-author-2e40db4c81b4-normal-deck-quot.title: Normal coverings and the convention-correct deck quotient

statement.heading: Statement
statement.source_excerpt: Let $p:(E,e)\to(G,x)$ be a connected covering and $H=p(E_e)$. A deck transformation is an invertible functor $T:E\to E$ with $pT=p$; deck transformations are multiplied by ordinary function composition, $ST=S\circ T$. They act freely on objects. Their action is transitive on a fibre (equivalently every fibre) exactly when $H$ is normal in $G_x$; such a covering is called normal. In this case $G_x/H\cong\mathrm{Deck}(p)$, with $aH$ sent to the unique deck transformation taking $e$ to the endpoint of the lift of $a$.

lem-author-2e40db4c81b4-pointed-classifi.title: Pointed classification of connected groupoid coverings

statement.heading: Statement
statement.source_excerpt:
A pointed groupoid $(E,e)$ is a groupoid with a chosen object $e$; a pointed functor sends the chosen object to the chosen object. For coverings $p:E\to G$ and $q:E'\to G$, a functor over $G$ is a functor $F:E\to E'$ satisfying $q\circ F=p$. An isomorphism over $G$ is such a functor with a two-sided inverse functor; it is pointed when it sends $e$ to the chosen object $e'$ of $E'$. A pointed covering $p:(E,e)\to(G,x)$ is a covering with $p(e)=x$. Unpointed isomorphisms over $G$ forget the chosen objects but still commute with the projections to $G$.

Let $p:(E,e)\to(G,x)$ be a connected covering of connected small groupoids and set $H=p(E_e)$. There is a unique pointed isomorphism over $G$ from $(C_H,H)$ to $(E,e)$. Consequently two pointed connected covers of $(G,x)$ are pointedly isomorphic over $G$ exactly when their characteristic subgroups are equal. Without chosen objects, equality is replaced by conjugacy in $G_x$.

lem-author-2e40db4c81b4-subgroup-cover.title: Explicit connected cover associated with a vertex subgroup

statement.heading: Statement
statement.source_excerpt: Let $G$ be a connected small groupoid, $x$ an object, and $H\le G_x$ a subgroup. Form objects $Ha=\{ha:h\in H\}$ for all arrows $a:x\to y$, recording $y$. There is a connected covering $C_H\to G$ whose arrows are pairs $(Ha,g)$ with $g:y\to z$, from $Ha$ to $Hag$, projecting to $g$. Its chosen object is $H1_x=H$ and its characteristic subgroup there is $H$.

lem-author-2e40db4c81b4-universal-cover.title: Universal groupoid covering from the trivial subgroup

statement.heading: Statement
statement.source_excerpt: Every nonempty connected small groupoid $G$, with a chosen object $x$, has a connected cover $U=C_{\{1_x\}}\to G$ with trivial vertex groups. Equivalently each morphism set between two objects upstairs is a singleton. Choose $1_x$ as the object of $U$ over $x$. A pointed connected cover of $(G,x)$ is called universal if it admits a unique pointed functor over $G$ to every pointed connected cover of $(G,x)$. The cover $U$ is universal, and each of these unique pointed functors from $U$ is itself a covering. A universal cover is unique up to unique pointed isomorphism, is normal, and has deck group isomorphic to $G_x$. Arrow products are read left to right, and deck transformations are multiplied by ordinary function composition.

lem-author-4ac39e6f1702-common-facet.title: Common relative facets have one enlarged standard subset

statement.heading: Statement
statement.source_excerpt:
In the finite-rank canonical Coxeter representation with simple-root basis $(\alpha_i)$ and dual space $\Theta$, fix $J$. Let $(x,I),(y,K)\in\mathrm{Cham}(J)$ be algebraic chamber labels such that $xC_I$ and $yC_K$ are adjacent relative chambers in $\Theta_J$, with common closed wall $F$. There are unique indices $a\notin I$ and $b\notin K$ describing this wall, and
$$F=\overline{xC_{I+a}}=\overline{yC_{K+b}},\qquad I+a=K+b=:L.$$
Here $I+a=I\cup\{a\}$, and closures are taken in $\Theta_J$. The two chambers lie on opposite sides of the supporting relative hyperplane of $F$.

lem-author-4ac39e6f1702-component-crossi.title: A finite connected component gives the opposite relative chamber

statement.heading: Statement
statement.source_excerpt: Let $(W,S)$ be a Coxeter system with finite generating set $S$, in its canonical real representation and dual chamber arrangement, and fix $J\subseteq S$. Let $(x,I)\in\mathrm{Cham}(J)$ and $a\in S\setminus I$ with finite $W_D$, where $D=[I,a]$. Set $L=I+a:=I\cup\{a\}$, $b=\iota_D(a)$, $K=L\setminus\{b\}$, and $v=w_{D\setminus\{a\}}w_D$. Then $(xv,K)\in\mathrm{Cham}(J)$, its chamber has the closed facet $\overline{xC_L}$, and it lies on the opposite side of its supporting hyperplane from $xC_I$. If this facet is the wall of a specified adjacent chamber, that chamber has label $(xv,K)$.

lem-author-4ac39e6f1702-component-opposi.title: Component opposition transports the retained simple roots

statement.heading: Statement
statement.source_excerpt:
Let $(W,S)$ be a Coxeter system with $S$ finite, in its canonical real representation with simple roots $\alpha_s$, Coxeter form $B$ and contragredient action on $V^*$. For $H\subseteq S$, write $W_H=\langle H\rangle$ and $C_H=\{f\in V^*:f(\alpha_h)=0\text{ for }h\in H,\ f(\alpha_s)>0\text{ for }s\in S\setminus H\}$. When $W_H$ is finite, write $w_H$ for its longest element and $\iota_H$ for its opposition permutation.

Let $I\subseteq S$, $a\in S\setminus I$, $L=I+a:=I\cup\{a\}$, and $D=[I,a]$, the vertex set of the connected component containing $a$ in the Coxeter diagram induced on $L$. Suppose $W_D$ is finite. Put $A=D\setminus\{a\}$, $b=\iota_D(a)$, $K=L\setminus\{b\}$, and $v=w_Aw_D$. Then $v$ maps the set of simple roots indexed by $K$ bijectively to those indexed by $I$. It fixes $C_L$ pointwise. For every $f\in C_K$,
$$(vf)(\alpha_a)=-f(\alpha_b)<0.$$
No finiteness assumption on the other components of $L$ is required.

lem-author-4ac39e6f1702-finite-crossing-.title: Adjacent relative chambers force a finite crossing component

statement.heading: Statement
statement.source_excerpt:
In the finite-rank canonical Coxeter representation, fix $J$ and let $(x,I),(y,K)$ label adjacent relative chambers $xC_I,yC_K\subseteq\Theta_J$. Let $a\notin I$ be the index of their common wall, and put $L=I+a=I\cup\{a\}$ and $u=y^{-1}x$. Then
$$\Phi_L^+\setminus\Phi_I^+\subseteq N(u),\qquad |\Phi_L\setminus\Phi_I|\leq 2\ell(u).$$
In particular $W_D$ is finite, where $D=[I,a]$ is the vertex set of the connected component containing $a$ in the Coxeter diagram induced on $I+a$.

lem-author-4ac39e6f1702-inverse-crossing.title: Componentwise crossings are inverse elements

statement.heading: Statement
statement.source_excerpt:
Let $I,a,D,A,b,K,v$ have the notation and finite-component hypothesis of component opposition. Then $[K,b]=D$, $\iota_D(b)=a$, and
$$w_{D\setminus\{b\}}w_D=v^{-1}.$$
Thus the two componentwise crossing elements multiply to the identity in either order.

lem-author-5a1e77100001-facet-incidence.title: Facet incidence and localized chamber signs

statement.heading: Statement
statement.source_excerpt: For the sign facets in *Sign facets of a cone arrangement*, write $F\preceq G$ when $F\subseteq\overline G$. This is a partial order, characterized by: every nonzero sign of $F$ equals the corresponding sign of $G$. Put $\mathcal A_F=\{H:F\subset H\}$. This is finite. If $C$ is a chamber, let $C_F$ be the chamber of $(I,\mathcal A_F)$ with the signs of $C$ on $\mathcal A_F$. For $F\preceq G$, one has $\mathcal A_G\subseteq\mathcal A_F$. If two chambers $C,D$ both satisfy $F\preceq C,D$ and $C_F=D_F$, then $C=D$.

lem-author-5f10a31d9e26-finite-ade-compl.title: The flop restriction complement is the finite ADE relative complement

statement.heading: Statement
statement.source_excerpt:
Work over $\mathbb C$ with the Axiom of Choice, retaining the complete-local smooth flopping setting and specified bundle choice of the slice-restriction contract. For its slice pair $(\Delta,J)$ and geometric arrangement $\mathcal H_\Lambda$, put $I=\Delta\setminus J$ and $n=|I|$, and index the coordinates of $\mathbb R^n$ by $I$. Use the finite ADE Coxeter system with the same labelled diagram $\Delta$, its canonical simple-root representation and the corresponding relative cone, arrangement and complement. The surviving-curve coordinates identify the arrangement $(\operatorname{Cone}(J)^\circ,\mathcal H^J)$ with $(\mathbb R^n,\mathcal H_\Lambda)$. They induce a homeomorphism
$$\mathcal X_J^{\mathbb C}\ \cong\ \mathbb C^n\setminus\bigcup_{K\in\mathcal H_\Lambda}K_{\mathbb C},$$
where $K_{\mathbb C}=\{x+iy:x,y\in K\}$.

Chambers are connected components of the real arrangement complement, and adjacency means sharing a wall in the chamber-and-wall definition. Here a chamber path is a finite nonempty sequence $(C_0,\ldots,C_m)$ of chambers with each consecutive pair adjacent, and its length is $m$. The coordinate identification gives bijections of chambers and chamber paths, preserves adjacency and path lengths, and therefore preserves minimum lengths for fixed endpoints.

$$\mathcal X_J^{\mathbb C}\ \cong\ \mathbb C^n\setminus\bigcup_{K\in\mathcal H_\Lambda}K_{\mathbb C},$$
where $K_{\mathbb C}=\{x+iy:x,y\in K\}$.

Chambers are connected components of the real arrangement complement, and adjacency means sharing a wall in the chamber-and-wall definition. Here a chamber path is a finite nonempty sequence $(C_0,\ldots,C_m)$ of chambers with each consecutive pair adjacent, and its length is $m$. statement.heading: Statement

Define the closed fundamental chamber by $x,y\geq0$ and the Tits cone by the union of its $W$-translates under the contragredient action. lem-author-7bd202611130-presentation-fai.title: The atomic-quadratic path quotient is faithful

statement.heading: Statement
statement.source_excerpt: Let $(W,S)$ be an arbitrary-rank Coxeter system with diagram vertex set $\Gamma_0$, and fix $J\subseteq\Gamma_0$. Let $Q$ have the associates of $J$ as vertices and one elementary edge $t_{a,I}:I\to K$ labelled by $v_{a,I}=w_{D\setminus\{a\}}w_D$ for each $a\in\Gamma_0\setminus I$ with $D=[I,a]$ and $W_D$ finite, where $b=\iota_D(a)$ and $K=(I\cup\{a\})\setminus\{b\}$. Impose all atomic braid relations on these edges and, for every such edge, both ordered quadratic relations $t_{a,I}t_{b,K}=1_I$ and $t_{b,K}t_{a,I}=1_K$, where $1_I$ and $1_K$ denote the empty paths. The reverse edge $t_{b,K}:K\to I$ exists under the same elementary-edge rule. Evaluation of labels induces a faithful functor from this path-category quotient to $\mathcal{BH}(J)$, and the quotient is a groupoid.

Impose all atomic braid relations on these edges and, for every such edge, both ordered quadratic relations $t_{a,I}t_{b,K}=1_I$ and $t_{b,K}t_{a,I}=1_K$, where $1_I$ and $1_K$ denote the empty paths. The reverse edge $t_{b,K}:K\to I$ exists under the same elementary-edge rule. Evaluation of labels induces a faithful functor from this path-category quotient to $\mathcal{BH}(J)$, and the quotient is a groupoid.

lem-author-9b7c42e8f103-chamber-topology.title: The full-cone and interior arrangements have identical chambers

statement.heading: Statement
statement.source_excerpt:
Let $(W,S)$ be a finite-rank Coxeter system in its canonical real representation $V=\mathbb R^S$, with basis $(\alpha_s)$, dual $\Theta$, root system $\Phi$, contragredient action, and Tits cone $U$. For $I\subseteq S$ put $E_I=\{f:f(\alpha_i)=0\ (i\in I)\}$ and $C_I=\{f\in E_I:f(\alpha_s)>0\ (s
otin I)\}$. Fix $J\subseteq S$ and put $E=E_J$, $T=U\cap E$, and $T^\circ=\operatorname{int}_E T$, the set of points admitting an open ball in $E$ contained in $T$. Write $H_\alpha=\{f\in\Theta:f(\alpha)=0\}$ and $\Phi^J=\{\alpha\in\Phi:E
ot\subseteq H_\alpha\}$. Let $\mathcal A=\{E\cap H_\alpha:\alpha\in\Phi^J\}$, $D= igcup_{K\in\mathcal A}K$, and $\mathcal A^\circ=\{K\in\mathcal A:K\cap T^\circ
e\varnothing\}$. Give $E$ its Euclidean topology and all its subsets their induced subspace topologies.

The identity identifies $T\setminus D$ and $T^\circ\setminus D$ as topological spaces, and hence identifies their connected components. Thus Iyama–Wemyss $J$-chambers, the sets $xC_I\subseteq E_J$ with $|I|=|J|$, are exactly the chambers of the restricted arrangement $(T^\circ,\mathcal A^\circ)$. Traces missing $T^\circ$ may be discarded without changing this conclusion.

lem-author-9b7c42e8f103-coordinate-faces.title: Coordinate faces span their annihilator subspaces

statement.heading: Statement
statement.source_excerpt: Let $V$ be a real vector space with finite basis $(\alpha_s)_{s\in S}$, let $I\subseteq S$, and put $E_I=\{f\in V^*:f(\alpha_i)=0\ (i\in I)\}$, $C_I=\{f\in E_I:f(\alpha_s)>0\ (s\notin I)\}$. lem-author-a7d202611130-finite-relative-.title: Finite relative longest element without spherical ambient rank

statement.heading: Statement
statement.source_excerpt: Let $(W,S)$ be a Coxeter system with $S=\{s_i:i\in\Gamma_0\}$, where $\Gamma_0$ may be infinite, and use its standard geometric root system $\Phi=\Phi^+\sqcup\Phi^-$. For $L\subseteq\Gamma_0$, write $W_L$ and $\Phi_L$ for its standard parabolic subgroup and roots, and put $\Pi_L=\{\alpha_i:i\in L\}$. Let $I\subseteq\Gamma_0$, let $a,b\in\Gamma_0\setminus I$ be distinct, and put $T=I\cup\{a,b\}$. Suppose $|\Phi_T\setminus\Phi_I|<\infty$. Let $D$ be the union of the connected components of the diagram induced on $T$ that meet $\{a,b\}$. Then $D$ is spherical, meaning $W_D$ is finite. With $w_L$ denoting the longest element whenever $W_L$ is finite, $r=w_Dw_{D\cap I}$ maps $\Pi_I$ onto $\Pi_K$ for an associate $K\subseteq T$ of $I$, and $q=r^{-1}$ is an article Brink–Howlett morphism $I\to K$ in the groupoid of associates of $I$. Writing $N(x)=\Phi^+\cap x\Phi^-$, one has $N(q)=\Phi_T^+\setminus\Phi_I^+$.

lem-author-a7d202611130-standard-minimum.title: Standard expressions are minimum generator words

statement.heading: Statement
statement.source_excerpt: Every standard expression of an article morphism $x$ is a minimum-length composable word in elementary Brink–Howlett generators, allowing inverse generators as well. lem-author-b19d43a8e520-bh-opposite-iden.title: Transfer to the root-action Brink–Howlett groupoid

statement.heading: Statement
statement.source_excerpt:
Let $(W,S)$ be a Coxeter system with diagram vertex set $\Gamma_0$, standard simple roots $\alpha_i$, and fixed $J\subseteq\Gamma_0$. An associate of $J$ is a subset $A\subseteq\Gamma_0$ for which $W_A$ is conjugate to $W_J$. Put $\Pi_A=\{\alpha_i:i\in A\}$. Let $\mathcal B$ have exactly these associates as objects and arrows $(B,x,A):A\to B$ when $x\Pi_A=\Pi_B$, with composition $(C,y,B)(B,x,A)=(C,yx,A)$.

An article arrow $x:I\to K$ corresponds to the reversed arrow $(I,x,K)$. Every article elementary label $v_{a,I}$ is a Brink–Howlett generator of this restricted $\mathcal B$, and every Brink–Howlett generator of this restricted groupoid corresponds to an article elementary label. No finite-rank assumption is imposed; the elementary labels require only their defining component $[I,a]$ to be spherical.

lem-author-b19d43a8e520-bh-parallel-root.title: Parallel classes of roots and finite inversion sets

statement.heading: Statement
statement.source_excerpt:
Let $(W,S)$, its ambient standard Coxeter roots $\Phi=\Phi^+\sqcup\Phi^-$, its root action and its length $\ell$ have the Coxeter-data conventions. Let $\mathcal B$ be the ordinary root-action groupoid on the associates of the fixed subset $J$, with arrows $(B,x,A):A\to B$ satisfying $x\Pi_A=\Pi_B$. At every object $A$ use the signed copy $\Phi(A)=\{A\}\times\Phi$, with $\Phi(A)^\pm=\{A\}\times\Phi^\pm$ and $-(A,\alpha)=(A,-\alpha)$. The arrow $(B,x,A)$ acts by $(A,\alpha)\mapsto(B,x\alpha)$. Thus the roots at an object are copies of the ambient Coxeter roots.

For an arrow $x:A\to B$, define $N(x)=\Phi(B)^+\cap x\Phi(A)^-$, identified with the ambient set $\Phi^+\cap x\Phi^-$. For $\alpha,\beta\in\Phi(A)$ put $\alpha\sim_A\beta$ if every arrow out of $A$ sends them to roots of the same sign. Call a root at $A$ real if some outgoing arrow changes its sign, and imaginary otherwise. Each $N(x)$ is a union of entire parallel classes at its codomain, all consisting of real roots. Arrow actions carry parallel classes bijectively to parallel classes. The set $C(x)$ of classes contained in $N(x)$ is finite; these are the inversion classes in the real compression of this signed root action.

source_references.title: Matthew Dyer and Harrison Gimenez, Root systems, Tits cones and imaginary cones of Brink-Howlett groupoids
source_references.statement: The standard Coxeter roots split into positive and negative roots; the ambient root inversion set Phi_w = Phi^+ intersect w(-Phi^+) has cardinality ell(w). Section 1.21 places a copy of these roots at each Brink–Howlett object. Realness means a sign change by some outgoing arrow; parallelism compares all outgoing signs; compression quotients by parallelism.
source_references.hypotheses: An arbitrary-rank Coxeter system with its standard based root system. The signed-copy and compression conventions apply to the specified root-action groupoid; the ambient inversion equality applies to every underlying element w in W.
source_references.reading_limits: Read HTML sections 1.3–1.4, 1.13, 1.21 and 3.1–3.4 for these statements and conventions. No PDF inspection, whole-paper reading, reconstruction of the imported inversion theorem or reading of Brink–Howlett (1999) is claimed.

statement.source_excerpt: Let $E=\Theta_J$ and let $B_E(u,r)$ be a relative ball supplied by the central-relative-ball lemma. lem-author-b319c70a2611-hyperplane-verte.title: A hyperplane near the centre separates opposite coordinate vertices

statement.heading: Statement
statement.source_excerpt:
Let $E$ be a finite-dimensional coordinate Euclidean space of dimension $d>0$, let $T\subseteq E$ and $u\in\operatorname{int}_E(T)$, and choose an orthonormal basis $e_1,\ldots,e_d$ and $\varepsilon>0$ with $p_i^\pm=u\pm\varepsilon e_i\in T$ and $B_E(u,\varepsilon)\subseteq T$. Every proper linear hyperplane $K\subset E$ meeting $B_E(u,\varepsilon/d)$ strictly separates $p_i^+$ and $p_i^-$ for some $i$.

Here a linear hyperplane means a linear subspace $K$ with $\dim_{\mathbb R}(E/K)=1$. Strict separation of $v,w\in E$ by $K$ means $a(v)a(w)<0$ for a nonzero real linear functional $a:E\to\mathbb R$ with $K=\ker a$. Such a functional exists, and the sign condition is independent of its choice, as proved below.

statement.heading: Statement
statement.source_excerpt: For a composable sequence of atoms $p_i=[I_{i-1},T_i,I_i]$ with $T_i=I_{i-1}\cup\{a_i\}$ finitary, put $g_i=w_{I_{i-1}}w_{T_i}$. statement.heading: Statement
statement.source_excerpt: Let $(W,S)$ be a Coxeter system and let $I,K\subseteq S$ be finitary, meaning that their standard parabolic subgroups $W_I$ and $W_K$ are finite. lem-author-c05e7a202611-rotation-words.title: Rotation parameters and the two switchback completions

statement.heading: Statement
statement.source_excerpt:
Let $(W,S)$ be a Coxeter system and let $T\subseteq S$ be finitary, meaning that $W_T=\langle T\rangle$ is finite. All the following constructions take place in the finite standard parabolic Coxeter system $(W_T,T)$. For $J\subseteq T$, let $w_J$ be its parabolic longest element and let $\ell$ be Coxeter length in $(W_T,T)$.

Use the following singular-expression conventions. Write $M(p)$ for the unique Bruhat-maximal element of a double coset $p$, using the Bruhat order of $(W_T,T)$. Let $*$ be the Coxeter monoid product on the underlying set $W_T$, with the Coxeter braid relations and idempotence $c*c=c$ for $c\in T$. For $p: J\to K$ and $q:K\to H$, where these arrows are respectively $(J,K)$- and $(K,H)$-double cosets, set $p*q=W_J(M(p)*M(q))W_H$. A singular expression $[J_0,\ldots,J_m]$ with successive subsets differing by one vertex denotes the composite of the double cosets $W_{J_{i-1}}eW_{J_i}$ in the displayed order. The notation $[J+c-d]$ records the path $J,J\cup\{c\},(J\cup\{c\})\setminus\{d\}$, with an addition required to add a missing vertex and a deletion required to remove a present one. An expression is reduced if each composition of a prefix with the next factor is reduced; a composition $p*q$ through $K$ is reduced when $\ell((M(p)w_K^{-1})M(q))=\ell(M(p)w_K^{-1})+\ell(M(q))$. Brackets with larger inclusions or deletions abbreviate the corresponding monotone single-vertex chains. In particular $[I,T,\bar I]$ means an inclusion chain from $I$ to $T$ followed by a deletion chain from $T$ to $\bar I$. An atomic expression concatenates the three-subset expressions of its atomic factors.

Let $T=I\sqcup\{a,b\}$ with $a\ne b$. Put $\bar c=w_Tcw_T$, $\bar J=\{\bar c:c\in J\}$ for $J\subseteq T$, $s=a$, $t=\bar b$, $u_{-1}=b$, $u_0=a$, $I_j=T\setminus\{u_j\}$ and $u_{j+1}=w_{I_j}u_{j-1}w_{I_j}$. Let $d=d(T,a,\bar b)$ be Ko's maximal index for which the rotation word is reduced. The first word $A$ consists, for $j=0,\ldots,d$, of the atomic steps $[L_j+u_{j-1}-u_{j+1}]$, where $L_j=T\setminus\{u_j,u_{j-1}\}$. The second word $B$ is obtained by reversing $A$ and applying $c\mapsto\bar c$ to every subset and vertex. Both are atomic reduced expressions from $I$ to $\bar I$. They express the same coset as the compressed expression $[I,T,\bar I]$. Their first added vertices are respectively $b$ and $a$.

lem-author-c73ab6d940e2-braid-congruence.title: Braid congruence preserves word length and support

statement.heading: Statement
statement.source_excerpt:
Let $S$ be any set and let $(m_{st})_{s,t\in S}$ be a symmetric matrix with $m_{ss}=1$ and $m_{st}\in\{2,3,\ldots\}\cup\{\infty\}$ for $s\ne t$. Let $S^*$ consist of finite words using only letters of $S$, with concatenation and empty word $\varepsilon$. For distinct $s,t$ with $m_{st}<\infty$, the braid pair consists of the two alternating words of length $m_{st}$ starting with $s$ and $t$; an infinite parameter contributes no pair. A congruence is an equivalence relation on $S^*$ stable under adding arbitrary left and right word contexts. Let $\equiv$ be the intersection of all congruences containing the braid pairs. Put $M=S^*/{\equiv}$, write $[w]$ for the class of $w$, and use multiplication $[x][y]=[xy]$ and identity $[\varepsilon]$. These operations are well defined and make $M$ a monoid, the presented positive Artin monoid. The length $|w|$ is the number of letters of $w$, and its support is the set of letters occurring in it.

Two words represent the same element of $M$ if and only if one is obtained from the other by a finite sequence of braid substitutions in word contexts. Every substitution preserves length and support. For finite $S$, this construction is the standard presented Artin monoid. For a spherical Artin system it therefore also gives the original conclusion for the positive submonoid of its Artin group, under the canonical identification with $M$.

lem-author-c73ab6d940e2-empty-ribbon-com.title: The empty-object ribbon component and its braid relations

statement.heading: Statement
statement.source_excerpt:
Let $(A,S)$ be a finite-rank spherical Artin system, so its associated Coxeter group $W$ is finite, and let $A^+$ be its positive monoid. For $I\subseteq S$, let $A_I^+$ be the standard parabolic submonoid generated by $I$ and let $\Delta_I$ be its standard Garside element, the positive lift of the longest element of $W_I$; in particular $\Delta_\varnothing=1$ and $\Delta_{\{a\}}=a$.

Use the ribbon category with objects $I\subseteq S$ and arrows $(I,g,J)$ satisfying $g^{-1}Ig=J$, with $g\in A^+$ for positive arrows and $g\in A$ for groupoid arrows. Equality requires equal endpoints and equal labels; composition is $(I,g,J)(J,h,K)=(I,gh,K)$. For $a\in S\setminus I$, the reduced generator has label $\nu(I,a)=\Delta_I^{-1}\Delta_{I\cup\{a\}}$ and target $\nu(I,a)^{-1}I\nu(I,a)$. The reduced positive category and reduced groupoid are the subcategory and subgroupoid generated by these arrows.

At $I=\varnothing$, every reduced generator is the loop labelled $a$. This object is an isolated component: its reduced positive component is the one-object monoid $A^+$, and its reduced groupoid component is the one-object group $A$. For distinct $a,b\in S$, the lcm for left divisibility has exactly its two alternating braid paths of length $m_{ab}$, and these braid equalities present this component as a groupoid.

statement.heading: Statement
statement.source_excerpt: For a spherical Artin system with standard generators $\sigma_s$ indexed by $S$, let $A$ be its Artin group. For $K\subseteq S$, write $w_K$ for the longest element of $W_K$ and $\Delta_K=\sigma_{w_K}$ for its positive reduced-word lift in $A$. Let $\iota_K:K\to K$ be the opposition permutation specified by $w_K e_i=-e_{\iota_K(i)}$. For every $J\subseteq S$, define $A_J^+$ to be the submonoid of $A$ generated by $\{\sigma_j:j\in J\}$, including the empty product, and $A_J$ to be the subgroup generated by the same elements. Then $\Delta_K^{-1}\sigma_i\Delta_K=\sigma_{\iota_K(i)}$ for $i\in K$. Consequently $\Delta_K^{-1}A_I^+\Delta_K=A_{\iota_K(I)}^+$ and $\Delta_K^{-1}A_I\Delta_K=A_{\iota_K(I)}$ whenever $I\subseteq K$.

lem-author-c81e5a0d2026-positive-support.title: Support of positive Artin words and longest lifts

statement.heading: Statement
statement.source_excerpt: Let $(A,S)$ be a spherical Artin system, with positive monoid $A^+$ and standard generators $\sigma_s$. The support of a positive element is the set of generator indices in any positive word representing it. This is well defined, and $\operatorname{supp}(xy)=\operatorname{supp}(x)\cup\operatorname{supp}(y)$. Write $A_I^+$ for the submonoid generated by $\{\sigma_i:i\in I\}$. Then $x\in A_I^+$ if and only if $\operatorname{supp}(x)\subseteq I$. For $I\subseteq S$, let $\Delta_I$ be the positive reduced-word lift of the longest element of $W_I$. Then $\operatorname{supp}(\Delta_I)=I$, including $\Delta_\varnothing=1$.

lem-author-c81e5a0d2026-reduced-ribbon-g.title: The reduced ribbon subgroupoid uses exactly the exterior atoms

statement.heading: Statement
statement.source_excerpt:
Let $(A,S)$ be a spherical Artin system, with positive monoid $A^+$ and standard parabolics $A_I^+$ and $A_I$ for every $I\subseteq S$. Use the ribbon groupoid $\mathcal R(A)$ with all these $A_I$ as objects, labelled by $I$, and arrows $(I,g,J)$ for $g\in A$ satisfying $g^{-1}A_I^+g=A_J^+$. Composition is $(I,g,J)(J,h,K)=(I,gh,K)$, the identity is $(I,1,I)$, and the inverse is $(J,g^{-1},I)$. Positive arrows have $g\in A^+$.

For $K\subseteq S$, let $w_K$ be the longest element of $W_K=\langle K\rangle$ in the associated Coxeter system. With $(e_s)_{s\in S}$ its canonical simple-root basis, use the opposition permutation $\iota_K:K\to K$ characterized by $w_K e_s=-e_{\iota_K(s)}$ for $s\in K$.

For the spherical Artin nu-structure, Godelle's subgroupoid $\mathcal R^\nu(A)$ is exactly the subgroupoid on this full object set generated by all arrows $r(I,a)=\Delta_I^{-1}\Delta_{I\cup\{a\}}:I\to\iota_{I\cup\{a\}}(I)$ for $a\notin I$, together with their inverses and every object identity. Thus it is generated by the exterior elementary ribbons, without the internal atoms $\Delta_{I_s}$ in the generating family. “Generated” permits finite composable products and inverses; it does not assert freeness or a list of relations.

statement.heading: Statement
statement.source_excerpt: In a spherical Artin system $(A,S)$, let $I\subseteq S$ and $a\in S\setminus I$, put $K=I\cup\{a\}$ and $J=\iota_K(I)$. Then $r(I,a)=\Delta_I^{-1}\Delta_K$ is positive, belongs to the positive ribbon category, and satisfies $r(I,a)^{-1}A_I^+r(I,a)=A_J^+$ and $r(I,a)^{-1}A_Ir(I,a)=A_J$. It is an arrow $I\to J$ in the left-to-right convention. Moreover $r(I,a)\notin A_I^+$. For $s\in I$, Godelle's other elementary atom $\nu_I(s)=\Delta_{I_s}$, where $I_s$ is the vertex set of the connected component containing $s$ in the induced Coxeter diagram on $I$, belongs to $A_I^+$.

lem-author-c81e5a0d2026-vertex-splitting.title: Unique conjugator factorization restricts to a normalizer splitting

statement.heading: Statement
statement.source_excerpt: Let $A$ be a group with specified subgroups $A_I$. Form the groupoid $\mathcal C$ with arrows $(I,g,J)$ satisfying $g^{-1}A_Ig=A_J$, and product $(I,g,J)(J,h,K)=(I,gh,K)$. Let $\mathcal P$ have only vertex arrows $A_I$, and let $\mathcal R\subseteq\mathcal C$ be a wide subgroupoid. Suppose every arrow $g:I\to J$ has a unique factorization $g=pr$ with $p\in A_I$ and $r\in\mathcal R(I,J)$. Then $\mathcal C=\mathcal P\rtimes\mathcal R$ in the internal sense, and $N_A(A_I)=A_I\rtimes\mathcal R_I$. Explicitly, every normalizer element has a unique such factorization, $A_I\cap\mathcal R_I=\{1\}$ and the action in the usual product coordinates is $\alpha_r(q)=rqr^{-1}$.

lem-author-d3116e202611-gallery-category.title: Positive gallery category, cancellation and length

statement.heading: Statement
statement.source_excerpt:
Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real vector space and $\mathcal A$ a finite set of linear hyperplanes in $V$ (a finite central arrangement). Chambers are the connected components of $V\setminus\bigcup_{H\in\mathcal A}H$. Assume every chamber is an open simplicial cone in $V$, meaning the set of positive linear combinations of some basis of $V$. A wall face of a chamber $C$ is an intersection $\overline C\cap H$ of dimension $\dim V-1$ with $H\in\mathcal A$; its supporting wall hyperplane is $H$, distinct from that face. Distinct chambers are adjacent when they share a wall face.

A gallery $(C_0,\ldots,C_n)$ has adjacent consecutive chambers and length $n$; a length-zero gallery consists of one chamber. It is minimal if its length is least among galleries with the same endpoints. Form the category $P$ with chambers as objects and galleries as arrows, modulo the path congruence generated by replacing any minimal subgallery by another with the same endpoints. Products follow traversal order, and empty paths give identities.

For every pair $A,B$, a minimal gallery exists and its class $u(A,B)$ is unique. Then $P$ is small, cancellative and atomic, with additive nonnegative integer length, length-zero arrows exactly identities, and atoms exactly one-step gallery classes. Here an atom is a nonidentity arrow admitting no factorization into two nonidentity arrows; atomicity means bounded lengths of factorizations of each arrow into nonidentity arrows. Reversal $(C_0,\ldots,C_n)\mapsto(C_n,\ldots,C_0)$ induces an involutive anti-isomorphism $g\mapsto g^*$. The antipodal map $(C_0,\ldots,C_n)\mapsto(-C_0,\ldots,-C_n)$ induces an involutive automorphism $g\mapsto-g$.

source_references.title: Pierre Deligne, Les immeubles des groupes de tresses généralisés, Inventiones mathematicae 17 (1972), 273–302
source_references.statement: Every pair of chambers has a minimal gallery of length equal to the number of separating hyperplanes. The rank-two replacements of (1.10) equate all minimal galleries with the same endpoints, and their gallery congruence admits cancellation on both sides.
source_references.hypotheses: A finite set of homogeneous real hyperplanes in a finite-dimensional real vector space, with every chamber an open simplicial cone in that space; composition follows traversal order.

lem-author-d3116e202611-gallery-cover.title: Gallery fractions, fundamental groupoid and asphericity

statement.heading: Statement
statement.source_excerpt: Let $Y=V_{\mathbb C}\setminus\bigcup_{H\in\mathcal A}H_{\mathbb C}$ for the finite central simplicial arrangement underlying the positive gallery category $P$. lem-author-d3116e202611-principal-prefix.title: Bounded prefix ideals and rank-two closure

statement.heading: Statement
statement.source_excerpt:
Let $V$, $\mathcal A$, $P$, and $u$ be as in the positive gallery category: $\mathcal A$ is a finite central arrangement in the finite-dimensional real vector space $V$, and every chamber is an open simplicial cone in $V$. Let $I$ be a set of arrows of $P$ with common source $A$ and bounded length; a prefix of $h$ is an arrow $g$ such that $h=gk$ for some arrow $k$, with products in traversal order.

A supporting wall hyperplane of a chamber $B$ is a hyperplane $H\in\mathcal A$ whose wall face $\overline B\cap H$ has dimension $\dim V-1$. For an intersection $Q$ of supporting wall hyperplanes of $B$ (with empty intersection $V$), let $F_B(Q)$ be the interior in $Q$ of $\overline B\cap Q$, the unique relatively open face of $\overline B$ with linear span $Q$. The residue at this face is the arrangement $\{H/Q:H\in\mathcal A,\ Q\subseteq H\}$ in $V/Q$. Let $B_Q$ be the unique chamber whose closure contains $F_B(Q)$ and whose residue chamber is opposite the residue chamber of $B$, and put $d_B(Q)=u(B,B_Q)$.

Then $I$ is the full prefix set of one unique arrow if and only if it contains $1_A$, is closed under taking prefixes, and whenever $g:A\to B$ and distinct supporting wall hyperplanes $M,N$ of $B$ satisfy $g d_B(M),g d_B(N)\in I$, also $g d_B(M\cap N)\in I$.

source_references.title: Pierre Deligne, Les immeubles des groupes de tresses généralisés, Inventiones mathematicae 17 (1972), 273–302
source_references.statement: For an intersection Q of supporting wall hyperplanes of a chamber B, the unique face supported on Q identifies its incident chambers with chambers of the quotient arrangement in V/Q; the opposite quotient chamber lifts to B_Q and Δ(Q)=u(B,B_Q). A length-bounded set I of gallery classes of source A is the prefix set of a unique class exactly when it contains the identity, is prefix closed, and contains gΔ(M∩N) whenever it contains both gΔ(M) and gΔ(N), for wall hyperplanes M,N at the target of g.

lem-author-d4ce11000001-directed-bigon-s.title: Doubling edges with bigons preserves the spherical space

statement.heading: Statement
statement.source_excerpt: Start with the spherical dual cell decomposition. Replace every undirected edge by two distinct directed one-cells in opposite directions, attach one bigon disk along their two-cycle, and retain one polygon disk for each dual face. Choose its cyclic boundary coherently with a fixed orientation of the sphere, using the directed edge on that face's side. The resulting finite cell complex is homeomorphic to $S^2$. There is one bigon for each undirected edge, not a second disk for a reversed cyclic reading of the same bigon.

lem-author-d4ce11000001-spherical-arrang.title: The seven D4 planes give a finite spherical cellulation

statement.heading: Statement

lem-author-e61520261113-finite-orbit-com.title: Finite equivariant Salvetti and orbit homotopy models

statement.heading: Statement
statement.source_excerpt: Let a finite group $G$ act linearly on a finite-dimensional real vector space $E$, preserve a finite arrangement $\mathcal A$ of proper linear hyperplanes, and act freely on $M=(E\times E)\setminus\bigcup_{H\in\mathcal A}(H\times H)$. With the natural good cover and its disjoint translates, there is a $G$-equivariant homotopy equivalence $f:K=\operatorname{Sal}(\mathcal A)\to M$ inducing a homotopy equivalence $\bar f:K/G\to M/G$. Both $K$ and $K/G$ are finite CW complexes, and $K$ uses the incident-pair order-complex convention. Here equivariance means $f(gk)=g f(k)$ for all $g\in G$ and $k\in K$; homotopy equivalence means ordinary homotopy equivalence, as in the comparison proposition. Orbit spaces carry the quotient topology.

lem-author-e61520261113-natural-salvetti.title: Natural finite Salvetti good covers

statement.heading: Statement
statement.source_excerpt:
Let $\mathcal A$ be a finite arrangement of proper linear hyperplanes in a finite-dimensional real vector space $E$, let a finite group $G$ act linearly on $E$ and permute $\mathcal A$, and choose facet points $x(F)\in F$ with $x(gF)=gx(F)$ as in *Invariant choices of facet points for finite linear symmetry groups*. Set $M=(E\times E)\setminus\bigcup_{H\in\mathcal A}(H\times H)$ with its subspace topology and diagonal action. Use the incident-pair poset $P(\mathcal A)$ of *The incident facet and chamber poset*: its elements are $(F,C)$ with $F\preceq C$, and $(F,C)\leq(F',C')$ means $F\preceq F'$ and $C_F\subseteq C'_{F'}$, where $C_F$ is the chamber of $\mathcal A_F=\{H:F\subset H\}$ containing $C$.

There is a finite $G$-invariant open good cover $\mathcal U=\{U(F,C)\}$ of $M$, injectively indexed by $P(\mathcal A)$, satisfying $gU(F,C)=U(gF,gC)$. Here a good cover means that every nonempty intersection of a nonempty finite subfamily is contractible, in the sense of *Nullhomotopic maps and contractible spaces*. Distinct members have nonempty intersection exactly when their incident pairs form a chain.

Define the abstract nerve $N(\mathcal U)$ to have vertex set $\mathcal U$ and simplices the empty set and all nonempty finite subfamilies with nonempty intersection. Write $\operatorname{Ch}(P(\mathcal A))$ for the abstract complex consisting of the empty set and the nonempty finite chains of $P(\mathcal A)$, and $K=|\operatorname{Ch}(P(\mathcal A))|=\operatorname{Sal}(E,\mathcal A)$ for the Salvetti realization of *The Salvetti order complex and its finite CW case*. The vertex map $U(F,C)\mapsto(F,C)$ gives a canonical $G$-equivariant simplicial isomorphism $N(\mathcal U)\cong\operatorname{Ch}(P(\mathcal A))$ and an induced $G$-equivariant homeomorphism $|N(\mathcal U)|\to K$, using the weak realization topology. The actions on the abstract complexes permute vertices, and on their realizations they permute barycentric coordinates.

lem-author-f758f7dd29a6-garside-transpor.title: Transport of a Garside structure to the presented monoid

statement.heading: Statement

lem-author-f758f7dd29a6-longest-lift-div.title: Both-sided divisors of the longest positive lift

statement.heading: Statement
statement.source_excerpt: Let $(W,S)$ be finite, let $M$ be the presented positive Artin monoid, and let $w_0$ be the longest Coxeter element. Put $\Delta=\boldsymbol{w_0}$ using the monoid reduced-word lift. A left divisor of $\Delta$ means $x\in M$ for which $xy=\Delta$ for some $y\in M$; a right divisor means $yx=\Delta$ for some $y$. The left divisors and the right divisors of $\Delta$ coincide, and both sets are exactly $\{\boldsymbol w:w\in W\}$. These elements generate $M$ and form a finite set.

Put $\Delta=\boldsymbol{w_0}$ using the monoid reduced-word lift. A left divisor of $\Delta$ means $x\in M$ for which $xy=\Delta$ for some $y\in M$; a right divisor means $yx=\Delta$ for some $y$. The left divisors and the right divisors of $\Delta$ coincide, and both sets are exactly $\{\boldsymbol w:w\in W\}$. These elements generate $M$ and form a finite set.

lem-author-f758f7dd29a6-monoid-reduced-l.title: Reduced Coxeter lifts in the presented positive monoid

statement.heading: Statement
statement.source_excerpt: Let $(W,S)$ be a finite-rank Coxeter system with length $\ell$, let $M$ be its presented positive Artin monoid, and let $A$ be its Artin group. Write $q:M\to W$ and $j:M\to A$ for the generator maps. For a reduced expression $w=s_1\cdots s_r$, set $\boldsymbol w=a_{s_1}\cdots a_{s_r}$ in $M$. This is independent of the reduced expression, $q(\boldsymbol w)=w$, and $d(\boldsymbol w)=\ell(w)$. Thus $w\mapsto\boldsymbol w$ is injective as a map of sets. Whenever $\ell(uv)=\ell(u)+\ell(v)$, one has $\boldsymbol{uv}=\boldsymbol u\boldsymbol v$. Moreover $j(\boldsymbol w)=\sigma_w$, the reduced-word lift in $A$. No injectivity of $j$ is assumed here.

lem-author-f758f7dd29a6-positive-degree.title: Positive degree and atoms of the presented Artin monoid

statement.heading: Statement
statement.source_excerpt: Let $M$ be the positive Artin monoid presented by generators $a_s$ and the braid relations associated with a finite set $S$ and a Coxeter matrix. A word is a finite string of these generators, and its length is its number of letters. Word length descends to an additive map $d:M\to\mathbb N$. It vanishes exactly on the identity, and the atoms (nonidentity elements which are not products of two nonidentity elements) are exactly the generators. Every element factors into atoms, and every factorization of $x$ into nonidentity elements has at most $d(x)$ factors. In particular there is no infinite chain obtained by repeatedly removing a nonidentity left or right factor.

lem-author-f758f7dd29a6-positive-image-i.title: Identifying the presented monoid with its positive image

statement.heading: Statement
statement.source_excerpt: For a finite-rank Coxeter system $(W,S)$, let $j:M\to A$ be the canonical homomorphism from the presented positive Artin monoid to its Artin group. Let $A^+$ denote the submonoid of $A$ generated by the positive generators. If $j$ is injective, it is an isomorphism $M\to A^+$. It carries $\boldsymbol w$ to $\sigma_w$ and, in finite type (that is, when $W$ is finite), $\boldsymbol{w_0}$ to $\sigma_{w_0}$, where $w_0$ is the unique element of maximal Coxeter length. A factorization in $A^+$ holds exactly when its unique preimages factor in $M$. In particular both divisibility relations, atoms and the additive degree are transported by this isomorphism.

lem-author-fcf1e9b45588-chamber-wall-ran.title: Chamber walls of an essential finite reflection group give full Coxeter rank

statement.heading: Statement
statement.source_excerpt: Let $W\leq\mathrm{GL}(E)$ be a finite real reflection group with essential action, in the invariant metric of [lem-author-fcf1e9b45588-invariant-metric-essentiality](item-lem-author-fcf1e9b45588-invariant-metric-essentiality). A chamber is a connected component of $E\setminus\bigcup_{H\in\mathcal A(W)}H$. A wall of a chamber is a hyperplane containing a codimension-one face of its closure. Let $S$ be the reflections in the walls of a fixed chamber $C$. Then $(W,S)$ is a Coxeter system, $W$ acts simply transitively on chambers, $|S|=\dim E$, and the wall normals form a basis of $E$.

source_references.title: Michael W. Davis, The Geometry and Topology of Coxeter Groups (author manuscript, August 2007)
source_references.locator: §6.6, Theorem 6.6.3(i)–(iii), printed p.89 (PDF p.105); setup printed pp.88–89; proof printed p.91
source_references.statement: For a finite group generated by linear reflections on a finite-dimensional real vector space, the reflections in the walls of a chamber form a Coxeter generating set S; the group acts simply transitively on chambers. If the action is essential, the chamber is a simplicial cone and |S| equals the dimension.

lem-author-fcf1e9b45588-invariant-metric.title: Invariant metric, product arrangements and essentiality

statement.heading: Statement
statement.source_excerpt: A finite real reflection arrangement in a finite-dimensional real vector space $E$ means the set $\mathcal A(W)=\{\operatorname{Fix}(r):r\in W\text{ is a reflection}\}$ for a finite subgroup $W\leq\mathrm{GL}(E)$ generated by reflections. Here a reflection is an involution with a codimension-one fixed subspace. A product arrangement on $E=E_1\oplus E_2$ consists of the hyperplanes $H_1\oplus E_2$ and $E_1\oplus H_2$ from arrangements on the two factors; a positive-dimensional empty factor is allowed. The arrangement is irreducible when it has no such decomposition with both $E_i\ne0$. For every such finite real reflection group $W$, the space $E$ admits a $W$-invariant positive-definite inner product. In that metric every reflection is the orthogonal reflection in its fixed hyperplane, and distinct reflections have distinct fixed hyperplanes. If additionally $\dim E>1$ and $\mathcal A(W)$ is irreducible, then $E^W=0$ (the action is essential).
